findings.title: Outbound netgroup-diversity set is built from ALL peers including inbound, so free inbound connections can veto our outbound replacement dials
findings.core_does: ThreadOpenConnections builds `outbound_ipv46_peer_netgroups` by switching on `pnode->m_conn_type` and explicitly BREAKS (contributes nothing) for INBOUND, ADDR_FETCH, FEELER and PRIVATE_BROADCAST, with the comment "We currently don't take inbound connections into account. Since they are free to make, an attacker could make them to prevent us from connecting to certain peers." Only MANUAL / OUTBOUND_FULL_RELAY / BLOCK_RELAY insert a group, and Tor/I2P/CJDNS peers are counted separately (outbound_privacy_network_peers) instead of contributing a group. The set is then used at net.cpp:2826 to reject a candidate in an already-occupied netgroup.
findings.we_do: replace-disconnected-peers computes `used-addrs` as `(mapcar #'peer-address (node-peers node))` — the whole peer list, inbound peers included — and `used-groups` from that, then at :665-667 skips any candidate whose /16 ip-netgroup is already in `used-groups`. Feeler, addr-fetch and block-relay peers are also folded in, and onion/i2p/cjdns peers are not carved out.
findings.impact: An attacker occupying inbound slots (114 by default, *max-inbound-connections*, and inbound connections cost the attacker nothing) from addresses spread across the /16 groups of our candidate list suppresses every outbound replacement dial to those groups. Because node-known-addresses is a static candidate list built once by connect-to-peers, covering its groups can drive replacement to zero while our outbound peers die off — the precise eclipse primitive Core's comment names. Even without an attacker, a busy node with many inbound peers silently blocks legitimate replacements that share a /16 with any inbound peer, so the outbound full-relay target is chronically under-filled.

findings.title: IsBadPort is absent: automatic outbound dials will connect to any gossiped port (SMTP, SSH, MySQL, IRC, …)
findings.core_does: ThreadOpenConnections rejects a selected addrman candidate with `if (nTries < 50 && (addr.IsIPv4() || addr.IsIPv6()) && IsBadPort(addr.GetPort())) continue;`. IsBadPort is an explicit deny-list of ~90 ports (1, 7, 9, 20-25, 53, 110, 119, 123, 143, 179, 389, 465, 512-515, 587, 636, 993, 995, 3306, 3389, 5432, 5900, 6000, 6667, 27017, …) documented in doc/p2p-bad-ports.md. Core also warns about them for -bind/-port (init.cpp:2135, 2169).
findings.we_do: There is no IsBadPort equivalent anywhere in src/ (grep for bad-port/IsBadPort returns nothing). select-dialable-address — the single filter every automatic selection path is required to go through (outbound slots, block-relay slots, feelers) — filters only on dialable-network-p and reachable-network-p; the port is passed straight to connect-peer. address-book-add likewise accepts any port, and relay-address gossips such records onward.
findings.impact: Any peer can gossip `victim-ip:25` / `:22` / `:3306` / `:6667`; we store them, select them, open a TCP connection and speak the Bitcoin protocol at an arbitrary third-party service, and re-gossip the address to two more nodes. That turns the node into an unwitting cross-protocol attack / port-scanning amplifier against arbitrary hosts (the exact scenario doc/p2p-bad-ports.md exists for), and wastes automatic outbound slots on addresses that can never complete a handshake.

findings.title: Gossiped addresses are relayed immediately, one addr message per address — no m_addrs_to_send queue and no poisson broadcast timer
findings.core_does: RelayAddress calls PushAddress, which only appends the address to the destination peer's `m_addrs_to_send` vector (capped at MAX_ADDR_TO_SEND=1000, with random replacement when full). Nothing is sent there. MaybeSendAddr later flushes the whole accumulated vector as ONE addr/addrv2 message and re-arms `m_next_addr_send = current_time + rand_exp_duration(AVG_ADDRESS_BROADCAST_INTERVAL)` (30 s mean, exponentially distributed, net_processing.cpp:160,5573), filtering m_addr_known on the same pass.
findings.we_do: relay-address ranks eligible peers and, inside the same loop, calls `(build-addr-response p (list peer-addr))` and `(send-message p msg)` — an immediate, single-address addr/addrv2 message per relayed address per destination. Grep confirms there is no addrs-to-send queue, no next-addr-send timer and no MaybeSendAddr equivalent anywhere in src/ (only the separate 24 h local-address self-announcement at protocol.lisp:2545+ has a timer).
findings.impact: Timing correlation: a peer watching our addr output sees a message the instant we accept a gossiped address from someone else, which is exactly the linkage Core's exponential broadcast timer exists to destroy — it lets an observer infer when and from where we learned each address and helps map our peer topology. Also multiplies bandwidth/message count (24-byte header + varint per address instead of up to 1000 batched) and gives a small per-message amplification: one 10-address addr from an attacker becomes up to 20 outbound addr messages.

findings.title: Eviction's disadvantaged-network reserve protects the NEWEST connections instead of the longest-connected (comparator inverted)
findings.core_does: ProtectEvictionCandidatesByRatio protects, per disadvantaged network, using CompareNodeNetworkTime whose final term is `return a.m_connected > b.m_connected;` — descending connect time — and EraseLastKElements then protects the LAST k, i.e. the SMALLEST m_connected = the longest-connected peers of that network. This is the same direction as ReverseCompareNodeTimeConnected used for the remaining uptime half (eviction.cpp:21-24, 175), and the file's comment says the point is to "protect the half of the remaining nodes which have been connected the longest … and precludes attacks that start later."
findings.we_do: %evict-protect-by-ratio calls %evict-erase-last-k with `(lambda (a b) (< (peer-connect-time a) (peer-connect-time b)))` for the per-network pass. %evict-erase-last-k (eviction.lisp:69-81) sorts and protects `(subseq sorted (- (length sorted) n))` — the last n. Ascending connect-time puts the oldest first and the most recent last, so the protected set is the most RECENTLY connected peers of that network. The final uptime pass two lines later (:167-171) correctly uses `>`, so the two passes disagree with each other.
findings.impact: The quarter of inbound slots reserved for onion / I2P / CJDNS / localhost peers is handed to whoever connected most recently. An attacker who repeatedly opens fresh inbound connections over Tor (or from localhost, or CJDNS) is guaranteed the reserved protected slots on every admission, while our long-established peers on those same networks fall back into the eviction pool — inverting the anti-"attacks that start later" property this pass exists to provide. The existing tests (tests/networking/dos-protection-tests.lisp:596, eclipse-dos-tests.lisp:1989) only assert that SOME onion peer survives, so they pass either way. This is distinct from the GA-known "inbound eviction protections" item, which was about the missing passes/k-values; the passes are present, one comparator inside them points the wrong way.

findings.title: Every dial counts an addrman failure — Core suppresses failure counting when the node looks offline, and never counts it for manual/addr-fetch dials
findings.core_does: ConnectNode calls `addrman.Attempt(target_addr, fCountFailure)` only `if (!proxyConnectionFailed)`. fCountFailure comes from OpenNetworkConnection, and ThreadOpenConnections computes it as `count_failures{((int)outbound_ipv46_peer_netgroups.size() + outbound_privacy_network_peers) >= std::min(m_max_automatic_connections - 1, 2)}` with the comment "Don't record addrman failure attempts when node is offline. This can be identified since all local network connections (if any) belong in the same netgroup." Every other OpenNetworkConnection call site — ADDR_FETCH/-seednode (:2422), -connect (:2541), addnode (:2986), addconnection (:1905) — passes `false`.
findings.we_do: %record-dial-attempt hard-codes `:count-failure t` and is called from establish-outbound-peer (which serves -addnode, -connect, -seednode and the addconnection test RPC), from replace-disconnected-peers and from do-feeler-connection. %record-outbound-result (:297) does the same on the failure branch. There is no online/offline test and no proxy-failure carve-out.
findings.impact: An offline episode (link down, laptop resumed, node started before the network is up, or a dead Tor proxy for the whole onion set) charges a real failure against every address we cycle through, on top of Core's own m_last_good epoch guard which limits it to one per address per epoch. A few offline/online cycles push nAttempts past ADDRMAN_RETRIES=3 with last_success still 0, at which point addr-info-terrible-p is true for the whole table: those addresses stop being returned by getaddr, become preferred overwrite targets in new buckets, and their GetChance collapses. Manual addnode/-connect targets that are simply down accrue the same damage, which Core never does. This is distinct from the GA-known "addrman failure accounting" item (attempts not being recorded at all from steady-state dials); the recording now exists but is unconditional in the direction Core deliberately gates.

findings.title: Block-relay-only eviction protection ignores fRelevantServices, so a non-tx-relay peer without the services we want can take one of the 8 reserved slots
findings.core_does: `EraseLastKElements(vEvictionCandidates, CompareNodeBlockRelayOnlyTime, 8, [](const NodeEvictionCandidate& n) { return !n.m_relay_txs && n.fRelevantServices; });` — the predicate requires BOTH that the peer does not relay transactions AND that it advertises all the services we want (m_has_all_wanted_services). CompareNodeBlockRelayOnlyTime also uses fRelevantServices as a tie-break.
findings.we_do: The same pass passes only `(lambda (p) (not (peer-relays-txs-p p)))` as its filter, and the comparator is plain last-block-time with no fRelevantServices tie-break.
findings.impact: Eight inbound slots are reserved for "non-tx-relay peers that have sent us novel blocks". Without the services conjunct, a peer that merely set relay=0 and forwarded one block — including a pruned/limited or witness-less node we would not otherwise value — consumes one of those protected slots, displacing a genuinely useful block-relay peer. Cheap for an attacker to arrange (relay=0 plus one block announcement), and it shrinks the effective protection this pass provides.

findings.title: address-book-add is missing Core's "do not update if no new information is present" gate and its nTime refresh interval
findings.core_does: For an address already in the table AddSingle first throttles the timestamp refresh — `const bool currently_online{NodeClock::now() - addr.nTime < 24h}; const auto update_interval{currently_online ? 1h : 24h}; if (pinfo->nTime < addr.nTime - update_interval - time_penalty) { pinfo->nTime = …; }` — and then bails out entirely with `if (addr.nTime <= pinfo->nTime) return false;` ("do not update if no new information is present"), BEFORE the fInTried / nRefCount / stochastic-multiplication checks.
findings.we_do: We bump last-seen on any strictly newer timestamp with no interval throttle (`(when (> time (peer-address-last-seen existing)) (setf …))`) and then fall straight through to the in-tried / ref-count-8 / `(ash 1 ref-count)` stochastic test and, if it passes, place the address into another new bucket. There is no equivalent of the `addr.nTime <= pinfo->nTime` early return.
findings.impact: A peer replaying an identical addr record (same, even stale, timestamp) keeps getting fresh rolls of the 1-in-2^refcount multiplication test, so it can push an address it controls up to the 8-bucket maximum in the new table without ever supplying new information — Core refuses the roll outright. The missing refresh interval also means our stored nTime tracks attacker-supplied gossip continuously rather than at most hourly, keeping otherwise-stale entries inside the 30-day ADDRMAN_HORIZON and out of addr-info-terrible-p. Bounded in practice by the per-address token bucket, hence S3.

findings.title: Inbound admission ban/discourage checks have no NoBan permission exemption
findings.core_does: CreateNodeFromAcceptedSocket guards both checks with the permission flag: `if (!NetPermissions::HasFlag(permission_flags, NetPermissionFlags::NoBan) && banned) return;` and `if (!NetPermissions::HasFlag(permission_flags, NetPermissionFlags::NoBan) && nInbound + 1 >= m_max_inbound && discouraged) return;`. The flags are computed from vWhitelistedRangeIncoming just above (net.cpp:1772).
findings.we_do: inbound-connection-allowed-p drops on `(peer-banned-p host)` and on `(and (peer-discouraged-p host) (>= (1+ inbound-count) *max-inbound-connections*))` with no consultation of peer-permission-flags, even though that function exists (netaddress.lisp:735) and record-misbehavior already uses +perm-noban+.
findings.impact: A peer the operator explicitly whitelisted with `-whitelist=noban@…` is still refused at accept time if its address happens to be banned or discouraged — the whole point of the option is that such a peer survives our opinion of it. Operationally this makes -whitelist=noban unreliable on shared/NAT addresses and on regtest/functional-test setups where 127.0.0.1 can get discouraged.

findings.title: -rpcpassword / -rpcauth / -rpcuser / -torpassword are written to debug.log in cleartext; Core masks them as ****
findings.core_does: AddArg tags -torpassword, -rpcauth, -rpcpassword and -rpcuser with ArgsManager::SENSITIVE (init.cpp:602/707/712/716). logArgsPrefix, which emits every `Config file arg:` and `Command-line arg:` line, does `std::string value_str = (*flags & SENSITIVE) ? "****" : value.write();` (args.cpp:883), so the secret never reaches the log.
findings.we_do: %log-args emits the raw JSON rendering for every KNOWN option, with no notion of a sensitive row: `(defer-log :info "Config file arg: ~:[~;[~:*~A] ~]~A=~A" ... name json)` (init.lisp:1490-1491) and `(defer-log :info "Command-line arg: ~A=~A" (car cell) (cdr cell))` (init.lisp:1497). Nothing in src/logging.lisp, src/config/ or src/node/init.lisp masks anything (grep for **** / sensitive / redact finds no masking code). -rpcpassword, -rpcuser, -rpcauth and -torpassword are all registered options (src/config-options.lisp:53,54,63,126), so known-config-option-p is true and they are logged.
findings.impact: A node started with `-rpcpassword=<secret>` (or with `rpcpassword=` / `rpcauth=` / `torpassword=` in bitcoin.conf) writes the plaintext RPC password, the rpcauth salt$HMAC and the Tor control password into debug.log at every start. debug.log is the file operators tail, ship to log aggregators and paste into bug reports; on Core the same command line leaks nothing. Anyone with read access to the log gets full RPC control of the node (and, via the Tor control password, of the local Tor daemon).

findings.title: A negated repeatable option (-noX) is appended to the list as the literal string "0" instead of clearing it; -norpcauth kills the RPC server, -noonlynet/-nodebugexclude refuse to start
findings.core_does: For list options (GetArgs -> GetSettingsList) a negation ERASES the span up to and including itself and blocks every lower-precedence source: `SettingsSpan::begin() { return data + negated(); }` (settings.cpp:264) where negated() is the position after the last `false` (settings.cpp:268-274), plus `done |= span.negated() > 0` (settings.cpp:240) and the prev_negated_empty gate at :243 that also suppresses the config-file "zombie" values. So `-rpcauth=a -rpcauth=b -norpcauth` yields an EMPTY list, and `-noconnect` with `connect=...` in bitcoin.conf yields an empty list too.
findings.we_do: interpret-arg turns any -noKEY into (KEY . "0") (args.lisp:52-53) and parse-cli-args keeps EVERY occurrence of a repeatable key (args.lisp:81-82). config-alist->start-node-plist then collects every value verbatim, including the "0" (node/args.lisp:35-39). There is no negation-clears-the-span rule anywhere in src/config/.
findings.impact: Concretely reachable from Core's own test suite. (a) rpc_users.py:178-181 restarts with `[-rpcauth=user1..., -rpcauth=user2..., -norpcauth]`; we build :rpc-auth = (user1spec user2spec "0"), parse-rpcauth-entry rejects "0" (src/rpc/server.lisp:750-764), %parse-rpcauth-credentials returns :invalid (src/rpc/server.lisp:1106-1113) and start-rpc-server returns NIL (src/rpc/server.lisp:1196-1198) — the node comes up with NO RPC at all, where Core comes up with RPC live and the two credentials revoked. (b) `-noonlynet` gives onlynets = ("0"), and conf-parse-network-name signals "Unknown network specified in -onlynet" (src/config/values.lisp:229) — startup failure on a command line Core accepts. (c) `-nodebugexclude` gives exclude = ("0"), and apply-log-categories signals "Unsupported logging category -debugexclude=0." (src/logging.lisp:445-447) — same. (d) feature_config_args.py:395 restarts with `-noconnect` against a bitcoin.conf that already carries `connect=0` (test_framework/util.py:580-581): we get :connect-nodes = ("0" "0"), which is not `equal` to '("0") (src/node/init.lisp:406), so instead of disabling outbound we log "Connecting only to -connect peers: 0, 0" and repeatedly try to dial a host named "0". The same shape means `-noconnect` on the command line does NOT clear a real `connect=<peer>` in bitcoin.conf — we keep dialing the peer the operator just disabled.

findings.title: The "-peerblockfilters without -blockfilterindex" refusal is nested inside (when prune ...), so an unpruned node advertises NODE_COMPACT_FILTERS it cannot serve
findings.our_ref: src/node/init.lisp:239-256 (the check at :253-254 sits inside the `(when prune` opened at :239)
findings.core_does: The check is unconditional in AppInitParameterInteraction and gates the service bit: `if (args.GetBoolArg("-peerblockfilters", ...)) { if (!g_enabled_filter_types.contains(BlockFilterType::BASIC)) return InitError(_("Cannot set -peerblockfilters without -blockfilterindex.")); g_local_services = ServiceFlags(g_local_services | NODE_COMPACT_FILTERS); }` (init.cpp:992-999). It is nowhere near the -prune block (init.cpp:1001-1008).
findings.we_do: %init-parameters puts `(when (and peer-block-filters (not blockfilterindex)) (config-error "Cannot set -peerblockfilters without -blockfilterindex."))` between the -txospenderindex and -reindex-chainstate prune checks, all inside `(when prune ...)`. With -prune absent the form is never evaluated. %init-peer-features-and-wallet then unconditionally does `(setf bl:*peer-block-filters* (and peer-block-filters t))` (src/node/init.lisp:837) — its docstring at :835 claims the gate happened in %INIT-PARAMETERS, which is only true under -prune.
findings.impact: `bitcoin-lisd -peerblockfilters=1` with no -blockfilterindex starts happily where Core refuses. We then set NODE_COMPACT_FILTERS in our advertised service flags (src/networking/peer.lisp:909-911), so BIP157 light clients pick us as a filter server, while %cf-serving-index returns NIL (src/networking/protocol.lisp:2147-2153) and handle-getcfilters/getcfheaders/getcfcheckpt silently return nothing. Every light client that selects us stalls on a request that is never answered and never rejected. Also a plain misconfiguration Core would have named at startup.

findings.title: Network-only options (-port, -rpcport, -bind, -connect, -addnode, -wallet, -walletdir) are honored from bitcoin.conf's default section on non-mainnet chains; Core ignores them AND refuses to start
findings.our_ref: src/node/args.lisp:281-287 (conf = sections then globals; merged = cli + settings + conf, first ASSOC wins)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/common/args.cpp:875-878 (UseDefaultSection), :134-146 (GetUnsuitableSectionOnlyArgs); refs/bitcoin/src/common/settings.cpp:181-184; refs/bitcoin/src/init.cpp:944-951; NETWORK_ONLY registrations at refs/bitcoin/src/init.cpp:539,548,550,575,708,713 and src/wallet/init.cpp:71,73
findings.core_does: `UseDefaultSection` returns false for a NETWORK_ONLY arg whenever m_network != "main" (args.cpp:875-878), which passes ignore_default_section_config=true into GetSetting/GetSettingsList, and settings.cpp:181-184 then drops the default-section value entirely. On top of that, GetUnsuitableSectionOnlyArgs (args.cpp:134-146) collects any network-only arg that is set ONLY in the default section, and init.cpp:944-951 turns that into a hard `InitError("Config setting for %s only applied on %s network when in [%s] section.")` — the node refuses to start.
findings.we_do: args->start-node-plist appends the [network] section entries in front of the global-area entries and lets first-ASSOC win, with no notion of a network-only option and no unsuitable-section check. A key present only in the global area is therefore applied on every chain. Nothing in src/config/ or src/node/ implements either half (grep for "only applied on" finds nothing).
findings.impact: A shared bitcoin.conf whose global area carries `rpcport=8332`, `port=8333`, `connect=<mainnet peer>`, `addnode=<mainnet peer>` or `wallet=<name>` silently applies those to a testnet4/signet/regtest node here. Core stops with a message naming the option; we bind the mainnet RPC port on a testnet node, or dial mainnet peers from a testnet node. This is exactly the accident the NETWORK_ONLY flag and the init error were added to prevent.

findings.title: -bind / -whitebind together with an explicit -listen=0 is accepted; Core makes it a hard init error
findings.core_does: `size_t nUserBind = args.GetArgs("-bind").size() + args.GetArgs("-whitebind").size(); if (nUserBind != 0 && !args.GetBoolArg("-listen", DEFAULT_LISTEN)) return InitError(Untranslated("Cannot set -bind or -whitebind together with -listen=0"));` — an explicit -listen=0 beats the -bind soft-set, and Core refuses rather than starting deaf.
findings.we_do: conf-effective-listen-flags replays Core's soft-set chain correctly (an explicit -listen wins over the -bind soft-set, values.lisp:319-321) and then only signals for the -listen=0/-listenonion=1 pair (values.lisp:333-334). The -bind/-whitebind case falls through: config-alist->start-node-plist still sets :listen-bind from the -bind value (src/node/args.lisp:84-89) and :listen NIL (src/node/args.lisp:118).
findings.impact: `-bind=127.0.0.1 -listen=0` starts a node that records a bind address and never listens on it. The operator's explicit binding is silently discarded where Core names the contradiction and stops. Same for -whitebind, where the discarded value also carried net permissions.

findings.title: Dotted section keys in bitcoin.conf (main.rpcport=..., test.connect=...) are treated as unknown options and dropped
findings.core_does: GetConfigOptions builds `name = prefix + key` (config.cpp:56) and ReadConfigStream passes it through InterpretKey, which splits the key at the first '.' into result.section + result.name (args.cpp:80-84) before the ro_config[section][name] store (config.cpp:109). So `main.rpcport=8888` written anywhere in the file — with or without a `[main]` header — is a main-section setting. Core's own argsman_tests exercises the dotted spelling directly (src/test/argsman_tests.cpp:788 builds `prefix = section + "."`).
findings.we_do: parse-bitcoin-conf-sections only recognises `[section]` header lines (conf.lisp:65-71); a key is taken whole and handed to interpret-arg, which strips a `no` prefix but never a `section.` prefix. `main.rpcport` therefore fails known-config-option-p and is reported by unknown-config-file-keys as "Ignoring unknown configuration value main.rpcport" (src/node/init.lisp:1567-1570).
findings.impact: An operator who scopes settings with the dotted spelling instead of section headers gets a node running entirely on defaults for those options. It is visible (one warning line per key) rather than silent, but a config Core reads and applies is one we discard.

findings.title: -forcednsseed=1 with -dnsseed=0 (or with -connect) is silently ignored instead of being an init error
findings.core_does: `if (args.GetBoolArg("-forcednsseed", DEFAULT_FORCEDNSSEED) && !args.GetBoolArg("-dnsseed", DEFAULT_DNSSEED)) return InitError(_("Cannot set -forcednsseed to true when setting -dnsseed to false."));` Because InitParameterInteraction already soft-set -dnsseed=0 for -connect / -maxconnections<=0 / a clearnet-free -onlynet (init.cpp:777-784, 833-842), this also fires for `-forcednsseed -connect=x`.
findings.we_do: The option row just sets *force-dns-seed* (config-options.lisp:338), and the only consumer guards on `(and *force-dns-seed* *dns-seed-enabled*)` (src/node/peers.lisp:352). No consistency check exists anywhere (grep for "forcednsseed" finds only these two sites plus the defvar).
findings.impact: `-forcednsseed -connect=<peer>` or `-forcednsseed -nodnsseed` starts a node on which -forcednsseed does nothing, where Core stops and tells the operator the two options contradict. The operator believes DNS seeding is being forced and never finds out it is not.

findings.title: A negative -maxconnections is accepted and clamped instead of being an init error
findings.core_does: `int user_max_connection = args.GetIntArg("-maxconnections", DEFAULT_MAX_PEER_CONNECTIONS); if (user_max_connection < 0) { return InitError(Untranslated("-maxconnections must be greater or equal than zero")); }`
findings.we_do: The option row parses the integer with no lower bound. automatic-inbound-capacity clamps the result with (max 0 ...) so inbound capacity becomes 0, and conf-effective-listen-flags separately reads `-maxconnections <= 0` as the -connect-style soft-set of -listen=0 (src/config/values.lisp:324-327). The node starts, listens for nobody and seeds no DNS.
findings.impact: A typo such as `-maxconnections=-1` (or a shell-mangled value) starts a node with no inbound capacity, listening disabled and DNS seeding disabled, instead of the immediate refusal Core gives. The node looks up but never gains peers, and nothing in the log names the cause.

findings.title: -rpcwhitelist / -rpcwhitelistdefault are accepted at startup but never enforced, so a user the operator restricted gets full RPC
findings.our_ref: src/config-options.lisp:404 (inside define-core-only-options, src/config-options.lisp:388); enforcement site missing in src/rpc/server.lisp:871 (rpc-handler) and src/rpc/server.lisp:411 (handle-batch-request)
findings.core_does: InitRPCAuthentication builds g_rpc_whitelist from every -rpcauth-authenticated user named in a -rpcwhitelist spec, and sets g_rpc_whitelist_default = GetBoolArg("-rpcwhitelistdefault", !GetArgs("-rpcwhitelist").empty()) (httprpc.cpp:306-316). HTTPReq_JSONRPC then gates EVERY request on it: a user with no whitelist entry while g_rpc_whitelist_default is set gets HTTP 403 for all methods (httprpc.cpp:144-148); a user WITH a whitelist gets 403 for any method not in it, checked both for the singleton request (:154-158) and for every member of a batch before any of them runs (:176-189).
findings.we_do: check-auth (server.lisp:800) returns the authenticated username exactly as Core does, and its docstring even says the name is returned "because Core threads it out of RPCAuthorized (httprpc.cpp:84) for -rpcwhitelist to key on" — but nothing ever consults it. -rpcwhitelist and -rpcwhitelistdefault are registered by define-core-only-options, i.e. parsed, accepted, and dropped. dispatch-rpc-method (server.lisp:68) looks up the method in *rpc-methods* with no per-user filter. Startup does emit one warning listing accepted-but-unimplemented options (src/node/init.lisp:1573-1577), so it is not literally silent, but the node still starts and serves.
findings.impact: An operator who follows Core's documented least-privilege recipe — an -rpcauth user for a monitoring/watchtower process plus -rpcwhitelist=monitor:getblockcount,getblockchaininfo — gets, on this node, a credential with the FULL RPC surface: stop, sendrawtransaction, generatetoaddress, setban, and every wallet method. The same command line on Core answers 403 for all of them. This is an authorization control that fails OPEN. The define-core-only-options docstring's reasoning ("accepting is not implementing" so Core-style command lines start) is sound for logging/cosmetic flags but is wrong for an access-control flag: for -rpcwhitelist, rejecting the option (or refusing to start) is the safe reading, and accepting -rpcwhitelistdefault=1 while granting everything to everyone is the exact inverse of what it asks for.

findings.title: /rest/spenttxouts serializes the on-disk compressed CBlockUndo codec instead of Core's REST format, and its JSON omits Core's leading coinbase array
findings.our_ref: src/rpc/rest.lisp:483-511 (%rest-spenttxouts), src/rpc/rest.lisp:506 calling bl.store:serialize-block-undo; src/storage/block-undo.lisp:34-70; src/rpc/rest.lisp:513-537 (%block-undo-json)
findings.core_does: rest_spent_txouts uses a REST-SPECIFIC serializer, not the rev-file codec: WriteCompactSize(vtxundo.size() + 1), then WriteCompactSize(0) as an empty list standing in for the coinbase, then per transaction WriteCompactSize(vprevout.size()) followed by `coin.out.Serialize(stream)` — a bare CTxOut, i.e. int64 LE nValue plus CompactSize-prefixed scriptPubKey, with NO height, NO coinbase flag and NO amount/script compression (rest.cpp:277-289). The JSON form likewise pushes an empty array first for the coinbase before the per-transaction arrays (rest.cpp:295).
findings.we_do: %rest-spenttxouts hands tx-undos straight to bl.store:serialize-block-undo, which is the DISK codec (its own file header documents it as Core's undo.h format): outer CompactSize is (length tx-undos) with no +1 and no leading zero, and each coin is written by bb-write-undo-coin as Core VARINT(height*2+coinbase), an 0x00 dummy byte when height>0, then bb-write-compressed-tx-out (TxOutCompression of value and script). The docstring at rest.lisp:484-489 asserts this is "Core's CBlockUndo serialization, which is the same codec the rev files use" — that is the mistake: Core deliberately does NOT use the rev-file codec here. %block-undo-json emits one array per non-coinbase transaction with no leading empty array.
findings.impact: Every /rest/spenttxouts/<hash>.bin and .hex response is undecodable by any client written against Core: the outer count is short by one, the coinbase placeholder is missing, and each coin carries extra leading VARINT bytes and a compressed (not raw) amount and script. A client that decodes it anyway reads garbage amounts and scripts. On the .json side the arrays are shifted by one, so a client indexing result[i] for block transaction i reads the coins of transaction i+1 — silently wrong prevout values attributed to the wrong transaction. Neither form errors; both look plausible.

findings.title: JSON-RPC batch members never get the named-argument transform, so any batch call using named params fails with -32603
findings.our_ref: src/rpc/server.lisp:411-431 (handle-batch-request), specifically the params binding at src/rpc/server.lisp:420-421
findings.core_does: Each batch member is re-parsed into the same JSONRPCRequest and executed through JSONRPCExec -> CRPCTable::execute -> ExecuteCommands -> ExecuteCommand, and ExecuteCommand applies transformNamedArguments whenever request.params.isObject() (rpc/server.cpp:508-510). Named parameters therefore work identically in a batch and in a singleton request.
findings.we_do: The singleton path (parse-json-rpc-request, server.lisp:303-305) calls (%normalize-rpc-params (%named-params-to-positional method ...)). The batch path binds params as (%normalize-rpc-params (or (gethash "params" req) '())) with no %named-params-to-positional call, so a member whose "params" is a JSON object reaches the handler as a raw hash-table. Handlers read positionally — (first params), (second params) — so (first <hash-table>) signals a type error, which handle-single-request's generic error clause converts to -32603 "Internal error: ...". Core's "args" positional-prefix convenience and the OBJ_NAMED_PARAMS options-object collection are likewise unavailable in a batch.
findings.impact: A client that batches named-argument calls (the shape doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md documents and that Core's own authproxy supports) gets an internal-error reply per member instead of a result. The failure mode is misleading: the error text names a Lisp type error, not a bad request, so the client cannot tell that the transport shape is at fault.

findings.title: No REST endpoint checks RPC warmup, so /rest/* serves a half-initialized node during startup instead of 503
findings.our_ref: src/rpc/rest.lisp:538-604 (rest-handle) and every %rest-* handler; contrast src/rpc/server.lisp:68-84 (dispatch-rpc-method), which does check
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/rest.cpp:170-176 (CheckWarmup) and its call at the head of every handler: rest.cpp:182, 314, 394, 501, 623, 717, 744, 783, 839, 898, 1093
findings.core_does: Every REST handler begins with `if (!CheckWarmup(req)) return false;`, which answers HTTP 503 with "Service temporarily unavailable: <rpcWarmupStatus>" for as long as RPCIsInWarmup is true — the same gate CRPCTable::execute applies to JSON-RPC.
findings.we_do: *rpc-warmup-status* is consulted only in dispatch-rpc-method, which the REST layer bypasses entirely: rest-handle routes directly to %rest-chaininfo, %rest-block, %rest-getutxos etc., and those call the rpc-* handler FUNCTIONS (e.g. (rpc-getblockchaininfo node nil) at rest.lisp:88) rather than dispatching. start-rpc-server binds the socket and installs the surfaces while warmup is still set (server.lisp:1186-1188), and warmup is only cleared at src/node/init.lisp:1237, after index catch-up.
findings.impact: During startup ("Loading block index...", "Replaying mempool...", "Catching up transaction index...") a REST client gets 200-with-content computed against a chainstate/mempool/index that is not yet consistent, or an opaque 500 from rest-dispatch-handler's catch-all, instead of Core's retryable 503 naming the phase. Monitoring and indexer clients that poll /rest/chaininfo on restart cannot distinguish "still starting" from "answered".

findings.title: /rest/block/<hash>.json renders getblock verbosity 2; Core renders verbosity 3 (SHOW_DETAILS_AND_PREVOUT)
findings.core_does: /rest/block/ is served by rest_block_extended, which passes TxVerbosity::SHOW_DETAILS_AND_PREVOUT (rest.cpp:472). In getblock that verbosity level is reached only at verbosity 3 (blockchain.cpp:867-874), and it adds a "prevout" object (generated, height, value, scriptPubKey) to every non-coinbase vin. /rest/block/notxdetails/ uses SHOW_TXID, i.e. verbosity 1.
findings.we_do: %rest-block calls (rpc-getblock node (list body (if notxdetails 1 2))) — verbosity 1 for notxdetails (correct) and verbosity 2 for the plain endpoint. Our getblock does implement verbosity 3 (blockchain.lisp:266-274, :prevouts (>= verbosity 3)), so the capability exists and is simply not requested from REST.
findings.impact: A REST client reading /rest/block/<hash>.json gets vins with no "prevout" member at all, so it cannot see the spent output's value, height, coinbase flag or scriptPubKey — the data that makes the endpoint usable for block explorers and fee analysis without a second round trip per input. The same request against Core returns them.

findings.title: getrawmempool ignores its second argument mempool_sequence, which our own argument table advertises
findings.our_ref: src/rpc/mempool.lisp:113-142; argument declared at src/rpc/core-tables.lisp:63 and src/rpc/core-tables.lisp:279
findings.core_does: getrawmempool takes (verbose, mempool_sequence). With verbose=false and mempool_sequence=true, MempoolToJSON returns an OBJECT {"txids": [...], "mempool_sequence": N} where N is pool.GetSequence() read under the same pool.cs as the txid list (mempool.cpp:588-605). With verbose=true and mempool_sequence=true it raises RPC_INVALID_PARAMETER "Verbose results cannot contain mempool sequence values." (mempool.cpp:574-576).
findings.we_do: rpc-getrawmempool binds only (first params) as verbose and never reads (second params). It returns a bare array for verbose=false regardless, and never raises the verbose+sequence conflict. The counter itself exists and works — bl.mp:mempool-sequence (src/mempool/mempool.lisp:430) is already read by the ZMQ sequence publisher (src/zmq.lisp:261-274) and by src/networking/protocol.lisp:2880,2930 — and core-tables.lisp:63/279 registers "mempool_sequence" as getrawmempool's argument 1, so a named call getrawmempool(verbose=false, mempool_sequence=true) is accepted, mapped to a positional slot, and then dropped on the floor.
findings.impact: This is the argument Core's doc/zmq.md tells a mempool-tracking client to use to take an atomic snapshot of the mempool together with the sequence number, so it can then apply ZMQ sequence events without a gap or a duplicate. On this node that client silently receives a plain array: result["mempool_sequence"] raises on the client side, or — worse — a client that tolerates the missing key falls back to "whatever sequence I saw last" and drifts out of sync with the mempool it is mirroring. The RPC advertises the parameter, so nothing signals that it was ignored.

findings.title: /rest/mempool/contents.json ignores the ?verbose= and ?mempool_sequence= query parameters and always serves the verbose dump
findings.core_does: rest_mempool reads ?verbose= (default "true") and ?mempool_sequence= (default "false"), rejects anything other than the literal strings "true"/"false" with HTTP 400 naming the parameter, rejects verbose+mempool_sequence together with HTTP 400 and a hint, then calls MempoolToJSON(pool, verbose, mempool_sequence) — so ?verbose=false yields a plain array of txids and ?verbose=false&mempool_sequence=true yields {"txids":[...],"mempool_sequence":N}. It also answers HTTP 400 (not 404) for a path other than info/contents (rest.cpp:787-789).
findings.we_do: %rest-mempool hardcodes (rpc-getrawmempool node (list t)) for "contents" — always verbose, no query-parameter parsing at all, no validation, no conflict check. (A malformed path does get a 400, which matches.)
findings.impact: A REST client asking for the cheap form gets the expensive one: on a full mempool the response is roughly an order of magnitude larger than the txid array it requested, and it is a different JSON TYPE (object keyed by txid rather than array), so the client's parse fails outright rather than degrading. Since /rest/ is unauthenticated whenever -rest is enabled, this is also an amplification the caller cannot opt out of. And, as with getrawmempool above, the mempool_sequence snapshot Core documents for ZMQ consumers is unreachable through REST too.

findings.title: getrawtransaction consults the mempool even when an explicit blockhash is given, and never rejects an unknown blockhash
findings.our_ref: src/rpc/rawtransaction.lisp:37-78 — mempool probe at src/rpc/rawtransaction.lisp:50, blockhash branch at src/rpc/rawtransaction.lisp:58
findings.core_does: Two things. (a) GetTransaction consults the mempool only when no block index was supplied: `if (mempool && !block_index) { ... }` (node/transaction.cpp:145). With a blockhash, Core looks in the txindex (rejecting a hit whose block_hash differs) and then reads that block, and nowhere else. (b) getrawtransaction resolves the blockhash first and throws RPC_INVALID_ADDRESS_OR_KEY "Block hash not found" when LookupBlockIndex returns nullptr (rawtransaction.cpp:301-303), before any transaction lookup.
findings.we_do: rpc-getrawtransaction probes the mempool unconditionally and returns the mempool transaction before it ever looks at blockhash-hint (rawtransaction.lisp:50-56). Only if the mempool misses does it try the hint. And when the hinted block is not in the block store it does not error — it falls through to the txindex branch and can return a transaction found in a completely different block, or ends at the generic not-found message.
findings.impact: getrawtransaction(txid, verbose, blockhash) is the query that asks "is this transaction in THAT block". For a txid still in the mempool we answer yes-here-it-is with no blockhash and no in_active_chain field, where Core answers -5 "No such transaction found in the provided block". For an unknown/typo'd blockhash we can answer with the transaction from whatever block the txindex points at, where Core answers -5 "Block hash not found" — so a caller using the blockhash argument as a containment check gets a false positive from both paths.

findings.title: coins-view-cache-sync clears DIRTY but leaves FRESH set, so coins already written to LevelDB are later dropped on spend without an erase
findings.our_ref: src/storage/coins-view-cache.lisp:369-372 (and the FRESH branch it feeds at :307-312, entered from :896)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/coins.cpp:291-300 (CCoinsViewCache::Sync) -> refs/bitcoin/src/coins.h:279-295 (CoinsViewCacheCursor::NextAndMaybeErase) and refs/bitcoin/src/coins.h:175-182 (SetClean); FRESH contract documented at refs/bitcoin/src/coins.h:150-159
findings.core_does: Sync builds a cursor with will_erase=false. For every flagged entry NextAndMaybeErase either erases it (spent) or calls SetClean(), which zeroes m_flags entirely -- BOTH DIRTY and FRESH. coins.h states the invariant verbatim: "Marking a coin as FRESH when it exists unspent in the parent cache will cause a consensus failure, since it might not be deleted from the parent when this cache is flushed."
findings.we_do: coins-view-cache-sync writes every dirty entry into the base LevelDB batch, then walks the table a second time doing only `(setf (ce-dirty ce) nil)`. ce-fresh is never cleared, and spent tombstones are left in the table rather than erased. The entry is now present-and-unspent in the base while still flagged FRESH in the cache.
findings.impact: %coin-view-iterate calls coins-view-cache-sync (coins-view-cache.lisp:896), and that is the path taken by gettxoutsetinfo, dumptxoutset, scantxoutset and the assumeutxo hash check (src/rpc/blockchain.lisp:1170, :1535, :1786; src/node/assumeutxo.lisp:290). After any one of those RPCs, every non-coinbase output created since the last full flush is on disk AND still FRESH. When such a coin is later spent, coins-view-cache-spend takes the ce-fresh branch, REMHASHes the entry and stages no erase, so the coin survives in the coins DB as unspent. The very next lookup of that outpoint re-fetches it from the base and reports it unspent, so a second spend of it -- in a later transaction of the same block, a later block, or after a restart -- is ACCEPTED. That is a consensus split (we accept a double-spend Core rejects) plus silent UTXO-set inflation; gettxoutsetinfo/hash_serialized_3 and any assumeutxo snapshot taken afterwards are also wrong. The existing regression test (tests/storage/storage-tests.lisp:1611) asserts dirty-count is zero after the sync but never inspects fresh, so it passes.

findings.title: %scan-flat-block-files stops at the first missing blk file, so a pruned node loses its entire flat block index on restart
findings.our_ref: src/storage/blocks.lisp:538-540 (`loop for file from 0 ... while (probe-file path)`), consumed by init-block-store:606-615 and rebuild-block-file-info:706-740
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/node/blockstorage.cpp:120-145 (BlockTreeDB::LoadBlockIndexGuts reads nFile/nDataPos/nUndoPos out of the block-index DB) and :529-610 (LoadBlockIndexDB); Core never locates blocks by scanning blk files except under -reindex
findings.core_does: Core persists each CBlockIndex's nFile and nDataPos in the block-index LevelDB and restores them at startup, so a hole in the blk numbering left by pruning is irrelevant -- every surviving file is still addressable.
findings.we_do: We rebuild the hash -> flat-file-pos map by probing blk00000.dat, blk00001.dat, ... and stopping at the first name that does not exist. The block index entries DO carry file/data-pos (src/storage/chain.lisp:30-31, persisted in the v2 header index), but nothing ever reads them back to populate block-store-index -- get-block goes through the scanned table only (src/storage/blocks.lisp:443, :518). The sibling undo scanner was fixed for exactly this hazard and says so in its own comment (src/storage/blocks.lisp:334-338: "Enumerated, not counted from 0 until one is missing: rev numbering has holes. Pruning deletes the lowest-numbered files first..."); the blk scanner was not.
findings.impact: prune-flat-block-file deletes blk/rev pairs lowest-number-first. After the first automatic prune, the next restart's scan stops at the first deleted file, so every block in the surviving higher-numbered files -- including the whole 288-block retention window -- is absent from block-store-index. get-block/block-exists-p return NIL for them, so the node cannot serve blocks, cannot read undo data, cannot reorg, and the coinbase-probe crash recovery (src/node/recovery.lisp:96-108) cannot find any committed ancestor. rebuild-block-file-info then produces an empty file-info table, so block-store-total-bytes under-reports and automatic pruning stops working. Worse, cursor-file/cursor-pos reset to the first surviving-or-recreated file, so once the write cursor rolls over (blocks.lisp:117-129) %store-block-flat opens an existing higher-numbered blk file with :if-exists :overwrite at offset 0 and writes over live block data. *flat-block-files* has been the default since 2026-08-26 (blocks.lisp:25-27), so this is the default configuration for a pruned node.

findings.title: The RPC coins sync advances the persisted coins best-block pointer without persisting the block index, so a later crash makes the node refuse to start
findings.our_ref: src/storage/coins-view-cache.lisp:365-366 (coins-view-cache-sync stages set-best-block) called from :896; compare src/node/flush.lisp:240-283 where the pointer is only ever meant to move as Phase 2 of the 3-phase commit
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/rpc/blockchain.cpp:1075 (gettxoutsetinfo calls ForceFlushStateToDisk(wipe_cache=false)) -> refs/bitcoin/src/validation.cpp:2780-2812 (FlushChainstateBlockFile, then WriteBlockIndexDB, then CoinsTip().Sync())
findings.core_does: Every path that syncs the coins to disk from an RPC goes through the full FlushStateToDisk, which flushes the block/undo files and writes the block index DB BEFORE syncing the coins, precisely so the coins DB can never name a block the block index does not contain.
findings.we_do: coins-view-cache-sync writes the coin deltas AND coins-view-batch-set-best-block for the cache's current block, but nothing on that path saves chainstate.dat or the header index. save-header-index has only three callers (src/node/flush.lisp:250 and two startup/reindex sites in src/node/init.lisp), so block index entries accepted since the last periodic flush are memory-only.
findings.impact: Run gettxoutsetinfo / dumptxoutset / scantxoutset, then crash or get OOM-killed before the next periodic flush (up to 600 s or 25 000 blocks later). On restart the coins DB's best-block names a block whose entry was never written to the header index, so reconcile-coins-db-best-block cannot place it and returns :unresolvable (src/node/recovery.lisp:38-46); src/node/init.lisp:812-815 then aborts start-up with "Refusing to start: the UTXO set names a block this node cannot place. Recover by reindexing from the block files, or restore a backup." A routine read-only RPC thus converts an ordinary unclean shutdown into a mandatory reindex.

findings.title: Pruning is not a flush trigger, so block files below tip-288 are unlinked while the on-disk chainstate can be thousands of blocks behind
findings.our_ref: src/validation/block.lisp:2710-2720 (maybe-periodic-flush, which is conditional, then prune-old-blocks unconditionally) and src/node/flush.lisp:329-361
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/validation.cpp:2714-2757 (FindFilesToPrune sets fFlushForPrune) and :2766-2812 (fFlushForPrune forces should_write; the UnlinkPrunedFiles at :2795-2800 sits inside the same FlushStateToDisk that has just written the block index and immediately goes on to sync the coins)
findings.core_does: Pruning can only happen inside FlushStateToDisk, and a non-empty prune set forces the write path: block/undo files are flushed, the block index is written, files are unlinked, and the coins are synced, all in one call. The chainstate on disk is therefore never more than that one function-call old relative to a prune.
findings.we_do: prune-old-blocks is called on every connected block, after a maybe-periodic-flush that fires only when its block-count / 600 s / cache-size triggers say so. Nothing makes a prune itself force a flush, so a prune routinely runs with the last durable chainstate up to 600 s (or +flush-every-n-blocks+ = 25000 blocks) behind the tip.
findings.impact: After a crash the coins DB is at height C while blocks up to T-288 have been deleted, with T possibly far above C. The recovery walk needs block bodies between C and T to find the highest committed ancestor and now cannot: src/node/recovery.lisp:178-180 emits exactly "no committed ancestor found on disk (blocks pruned below the UTXO tip?); resync required" and the node aborts for a full resync. The same gap also leaves chain-state-pruned-height above best-height, which stalls further pruning (prune-old-blocks returns 0 when min-keep-height <= start).

findings.title: The prune window's lower bound is our walk cursor rather than Core's 0, so the first blk file is never prunable
findings.our_ref: src/storage/blocks.lisp:889 (`(%prunable-flat-files store (1+ start) min-keep-height)`) with start from src/storage/chain.lisp:201-207 and pruned-height defaulting to 0 at chain.lisp:57
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/validation.cpp:6366-6391 (Chainstate::GetPruneRange returns prune_start = 0 unless this is an unvalidated snapshot chainstate) and refs/bitcoin/src/node/blockstorage.cpp:386-389 (`if (fileinfo.nHeightLast > last_block_can_prune || fileinfo.nHeightFirst < min_block_to_prune) continue;`)
findings.core_does: min_block_to_prune is 0 for an ordinary chainstate, so a file whose nHeightFirst is 0 (the one containing genesis) satisfies `nHeightFirst < 0` == false and is pruned like any other once its nHeightLast falls inside the window.
findings.we_do: We pass (1+ chain-state-prune-walk-start) as the window floor. With pruned-height starting at 0 that floor is 1, and blk00000.dat -- whose height-first is 0 because ensure-genesis-on-disk writes genesis into it -- fails the `(>= first min-height)` test forever. It is skipped on every subsequent prune too, since the floor only rises.
findings.impact: A pruned node permanently retains its first blk/rev pair (up to +max-blockfile-size+ = 128 MiB plus its undo file) above the configured -prune target, so actual disk use exceeds the target by that amount for the life of the datadir. It also guarantees blk00000.dat always exists, which is what shapes the failure mode of the scanner bug above (the scan always finds file 0 and then stops at the first pruned file).

findings.title: testmempoolaccept validates each transaction in isolation; Core runs multi-tx batches as a package, so a CPFP child is falsely reported "missing-inputs"
findings.core_does: For `txns.size() > 1`, testmempoolaccept calls `ProcessNewPackage(..., test_accept=true)` -> `AcceptMultipleTransactionsInternal` with `ATMPArgs::PackageTestAccept` (validation.cpp:497-513). That path runs `IsWellFormedPackage` first (count/weight/topo-sort/no-conflicts) and reports a package-level failure via a `package-error` field on every row; after each member's PreChecks it calls `m_viewmempool.PackageAddTransaction(ws.m_ptx)` (validation.cpp:1473) so a later member CAN spend an earlier member's not-yet-in-mempool output; it sets `allow_replacement=false` so a member conflicting with a mempool tx gets "bip125-replacement-disallowed"; and it emits `reject-details` plus "validation unfinished" (txid/wtxid only) rows for members with no result.
findings.we_do: The handler decodes the batch, then loops `(dolist (tx decoded ...)` calling `bl.val:validate-transaction-for-mempool` on each tx independently against the live UTXO set + mempool, with no `package-coins`, no `package-well-formed` check, no `package-error` field and no `reject-details`. The docstring states the divergence outright: "Each tx is checked independently against current state (package interdependence is not modeled -- that needs submitpackage)". The machinery to do it correctly already exists next door (`bl.val:validate-package-for-mempool`, src/validation/packages.lisp:549).
findings.impact: Any caller dry-running a 1-parent-1-child (CPFP / LN anchor) package before broadcasting gets `allowed:false, reject-reason:"missing-inputs"` for the child, where Core answers `allowed:true` with the package effective-feerate and `effective-includes` listing both wtxids. Wallets and LN implementations that gate submitpackage on testmempoolaccept will refuse to broadcast valid packages. A malformed package (unsorted, internally conflicting, over MAX_PACKAGE_WEIGHT) also gets per-tx verdicts instead of Core's package-error, and a member conflicting with the mempool is reported acceptable where Core says bip125-replacement-disallowed.

findings.title: Fee estimator has no `validForFeeEstimation` gate: it tracks reorg re-adds, package submissions, chained children, and transactions accepted while the node is behind
findings.core_does: `CBlockPolicyEstimator::processTransaction` drops the transaction unless every one of five conditions holds: `txHeight == nBestSeenHeight` (:607, ignore side chains / an estimator not yet synced to the tip) and `validForFeeEstimation = !m_mempool_limit_bypassed && !m_submitted_in_package && m_chainstate_is_current && m_has_no_mempool_parents` (:619). Those four flags are supplied at the call site by `NewMempoolTransactionInfo(..., args.m_bypass_limits, args.m_package_submission, IsCurrentForFeeEstimation(m_active_chainstate), m_pool.HasNoInputsOf(tx))` (validation.cpp:1305-1308). Excluded transactions bump `untrackedTxs` and are never bucketed.
findings.we_do: `accept-validated-tx` calls `(bpe-note-entry txid fee vsize height)` for EVERY acceptance that returns :ok -- including the reorg re-add path (`readd-disconnected-txs-to-mempool`, which passes :bypass-limits t), package submission (`%accept-into-mempool`), mempool.dat reload, and transactions with in-mempool parents. `bpe-process-transaction` applies no filter at all: it only skips a txid already tracked, then buckets the feerate into all three horizons. There is no `IsCurrentForFeeEstimation` analogue anywhere in the tree (grep for "current-for-fee" returns nothing), no `has-no-mempool-parents` test, and no `height == best-seen-height` guard.
findings.impact: estimatesmartfee/estimaterawfee are systematically biased away from Core. Chained children are the common case Core most cares about excluding: a CPFP child's confirmation delay is set by its parent's chunk position, so a high-feerate child that waits records as "high feerate, slow" (pushing estimates up) and a low-feerate parent dragged in by its child records as "low feerate, fast" (pushing estimates down). Accepting transactions while the tip is stale (post-restart catch-up, or a chain a few hours behind) then seeing several blocks arrive in quick succession teaches the long horizon -- half-life one week -- that very low feerates confirm within one or two blocks, so the wallet underpays and its transactions stall.

findings.title: Rolling minimum fee decays with no block since the bump, and block connection never resets the decay clock
findings.core_does: `trackPackageRemoved` raises `rollingMinimumFeeRate` and sets `blockSinceLastRollingFeeBump = false` (:855-857). `GetMinFee` then returns the UNDECAYED rate while that flag is false (:831-832) -- the floor is frozen at the level of what was just trimmed until a block arrives, which is exactly the property TrimToSize's comment asks for ("we don't allow txn to enter mempool with feerate equal to txn which were removed with no block in between"). `removeForBlock` sets `lastRollingFeeUpdate = GetTime()` and `blockSinceLastRollingFeeBump = true` (:426-427), and `GetMinFee` mutates `rollingMinimumFeeRate`/`lastRollingFeeUpdate` in place each time it decays, so the half-life in force is applied piecewise over time as pool usage changes.
findings.we_do: `mempool-trim-to-size` sets `rolling-min-fee-rate` and `rolling-min-fee-time` to now; there is no `block-since-last-rolling-fee-bump` slot at all, so decay starts the instant the bump happens. `mempool-remove-for-block` never touches `rolling-min-fee-time`. `mempool-decayed-rolling-min-fee-rate` recomputes `rolling * 0.5^(age/halflife)` from the ORIGINAL anchor without writing back, and selects the half-life from the pool's usage AT READ TIME, applying that one half-life retroactively across the whole age.
findings.impact: Two effects, both loosening the anti-churn floor relative to Core. (1) After a trim, transactions at the feerate just evicted are admitted again immediately (decayed) rather than being held out until a block; on a testnet or during a long inter-block gap this reopens the eviction churn the mechanism exists to damp. (2) A pool that trims while full and later drains below a quarter of the cap has the 3-hour half-life applied to the entire elapsed period including the hours it was full, so the floor collapses far faster than Core's piecewise decay. getmempoolinfo's mempoolminfee and the BIP133 feefilter we advertise both read low as a result.

findings.title: The relay-finality check runs after the duplicate and missing-input checks, so a non-final transaction with unknown parents is stored in the orphanage instead of rejected
findings.core_does: PreChecks runs `CheckFinalTxAtTip` at :819 -- immediately after the tx-size-small check and BEFORE the `m_pool.exists` duplicate test (:823) and before the coin-availability loop that yields TX_MISSING_INPUTS (:866). A non-final transaction therefore always fails with TX_PREMATURE_SPEND / "non-final", which net_processing caches by wtxid and never treats as an orphan.
findings.we_do: The order is duplicate-in-mempool (:1088), then `mempool-extra-coins` -> `:missing-input` (:1097-1128), and only then the finality and BIP68 block (:1130-1144). A transaction that is both non-final and references outputs we do not have returns `:missing-input`.
findings.impact: `:missing-input` is the orphan trigger in src/networking/protocol.lisp:1778ff: we store the transaction in the orphan pool and issue getdata for its (possibly nonexistent) parents, where Core drops it outright and remembers the wtxid. Non-final orphans consume orphanage weight/latency budget and parent-fetch slots that Core never spends. The reject reason reported by sendrawtransaction/testmempoolaccept is also "missing-inputs" where Core says "non-final", which Core's own functional suite matches on.

findings.title: CheckTxInputs (coinbase maturity, fee/value consensus) runs after the standardness-of-inputs, sigop and witness checks instead of before
findings.core_does: PreChecks runs `Consensus::CheckTxInputs` FIRST at :892 (yielding "bad-txns-premature-spend-of-coinbase", "bad-txns-in-belowout", "bad-txns-fee-outofrange", all TX_CONSENSUS), and only then `AreInputsStandard` (:896, TX_INPUTS_NOT_STANDARD), `IsWitnessStandard` (:901, TX_WITNESS_MUTATED), and `GetTransactionSigOpCost` (:905) whose cap is enforced later at :938.
findings.we_do: The `flet`-wrapped block runs `are-inputs-standard-p` -> `:nonstandard-inputs` (:1166), then the MAX_STANDARD_TX_SIGOPS_COST cap -> `:too-many-sigops` (:1171), then `is-witness-standard-p` -> `:bad-witness-nonstandard` (:1179), and only afterwards `validate-transaction-contextual` (:1195) which is our CheckTxInputs. The witness/sigop order is also swapped relative to Core (Core checks IsWitnessStandard at :901 before computing sigop cost at :905).
findings.impact: A transaction that fails two of these at once is reported with the wrong reason. Concretely: an immature-coinbase spend whose spent scriptPubKey is also nonstandard reports "bad-txns-nonstandard-inputs" (a policy result) instead of Core's "bad-txns-premature-spend-of-coinbase" (a consensus result); and a witness-nonstandard spend that is also sigop-dense reports "bad-txns-too-many-sigops" instead of "bad-witness-nonstandard". The reject vocabulary is what Core's functional suite and package-relay peers key on, and our own reject-cache policy branches on `:nonstandard-inputs` (txid+wtxid) versus the rest (wtxid only), so the swap can change which identifiers get cached.

findings.title: Duplicate-in-mempool check is txid-only: Core's "txn-same-nonwitness-data-in-mempool" case is never reported
findings.core_does: Two separate probes in order: `m_pool.exists(tx.GetWitnessHash())` -> TX_CONFLICT "txn-already-in-mempool" (the byte-identical transaction), else `m_pool.exists(tx.GetHash())` -> TX_CONFLICT "txn-same-nonwitness-data-in-mempool" (same txid, different witness -- a witness-malleated variant of something we already hold).
findings.we_do: A single `(bl.mp:mempool-has mempool txid)` probe returning `:already-in-mempool`, which `tx-reject-reason-string` renders as "txn-already-in-mempool" (src/validation/transaction.lisp:905). The wtxid index exists (`mempool-get-by-wtxid`, src/mempool/mempool.lisp:621) but is not consulted here.
findings.impact: Both paths reject, so there is no acceptance divergence, but a peer or RPC client that submits a witness-malleated duplicate is told the exact transaction is already pooled rather than that we hold a same-txid-different-witness variant. Core's functional suite and any client distinguishing genuine duplicate submission from witness malleation reads that as a divergence, and the distinction is the only signal that malleation is occurring.

findings.title: Package consistency check adds inputs one at a time, misreporting a transaction with duplicate inputs as a package conflict; empty-vin members are not caught
findings.core_does: `IsConsistentPackage` returns false immediately if any `tx->vin` is empty (:56-62, with the comment that duplicate empty transactions are also inconsistent), and it deliberately BATCH-adds each transaction's prevouts only after checking them all: "If we added them 1 at a time, we could catch duplicate inputs within a single tx. This is a more severe, consensus error, and we want to report that from CheckTransaction instead."
findings.we_do: The loop does `(when (gethash key spent) ... :conflict-in-package)` and `(setf (gethash key spent) t)` inside the same per-input iteration, so a single transaction that spends one outpoint twice collides with itself. An empty-inputs member contributes nothing and passes.
findings.impact: A submitpackage containing a transaction with a duplicated input is rejected package-wide as `:conflict-in-package` (a PCKG_POLICY-level verdict, no per-member results) where Core lets it reach CheckTransaction and reports the per-transaction consensus error "bad-txns-inputs-duplicate". An empty-vin member likewise surfaces as a per-tx structure error rather than Core's package-level "conflict-in-package". Callers cannot tell which member is at fault in the first case.

findings.title: Block-conflict removal does not clear the conflicted transaction's prioritisation delta
findings.core_does: `removeConflicts` calls `ClearPrioritisation(txConflict.GetHash())` before `removeRecursive(it->second, MemPoolRemovalReason::CONFLICT)` for every mempool transaction spending an outpoint the block just consumed -- the delta is dropped along with the transaction it was attached to.
findings.we_do: `mempool-remove-for-block` clears the delta only for CONFIRMED block transactions (`(remhash txid (mempool-deltas mempool))` in the :block branch). The :conflict branch just calls `mempool-remove-recursive`, leaving the conflicted transaction's entry in `mempool-deltas`.
findings.impact: A prioritisetransaction delta applied to a transaction that a block then double-spends survives in the deltas map forever (it is only re-consumed if that exact txid is ever re-submitted, which a conflicted transaction never can be). It leaks into `mempool-dynamic-usage` accounting (+usage-per-delta+ per residual entry), into getprioritisedtransactions output, and into the mempool.dat residual-delta section on every dump, where it is reloaded on restart.

findings.title: Re-mined transactions are never removed from the reorg disconnect pool, so their still-valid in-mempool children are removed recursively
findings.core_does: ConnectTip does `m_mempool->removeForBlock(block_to_connect->vtx, ...)` AND `disconnectpool.removeForBlock(block_to_connect->vtx)`. A transaction that was in the old chain and is re-mined in the new chain is therefore deleted from the disconnect pool and never reaches MaybeUpdateMempoolForReorg's `removeRecursive` arm.
findings.we_do: %REORG-DISCONNECT pushes every non-coinbase tx of every disconnected block into REORG-DISCONNECTED-BLOCK-TXS, and nothing ever removes the ones re-mined by the fork. %REORG-COMMIT's connected loop calls only `mempool-remove-for-block` (3362); then line 3394 hands the *entire* pool to READD-DISCONNECTED-TXS-TO-MEMPOOL. For a re-mined tx P, `validate-transaction-for-mempool` fails (P's inputs are already spent by P itself in the connected block) and `mempool-has` is false, so block.lisp:2895-2898 runs `mempool-remove-spenders P (n-outputs)`.
findings.impact: After any reorg that re-mines a transaction — the normal outcome of a 1-2 block reorg — every mempool transaction spending an output of a re-mined tx is evicted with its descendants, even though its parent is confirmed on the new chain and the child is perfectly valid. Unconfirmed CPFP/chained wallet spends silently vanish from the mempool and are not re-relayed. Core keeps them.

findings.title: REORG-DISCONNECTED-BLOCKS retains every disconnected block in full, defeating the 20 MB disconnect-pool cap
findings.core_does: DisconnectTip reads the block into a local shared_ptr, fires BlockDisconnected, and lets it go; only DisconnectedBlockTransactions retains transactions and it is hard-capped at MAX_DISCONNECTED_TX_POOL_BYTES. InvalidateBlock additionally calls LimitValidationInterfaceQueue each iteration so the queued signal payloads cannot grow unboundedly either.
findings.we_do: PHASE A defers all notifications to PHASE C, so it pushes `(cons block height)` for EVERY disconnected block onto REORG-DISCONNECTED-BLOCKS with no bound. The `trim-disconnect-pool` cap at 3155-3160 drops only the parallel tx lists — the identical transaction objects stay reachable through REORG-DISCONNECTED-BLOCKS, so the 20 MB budget bounds nothing.
findings.impact: A deep rollback pins every disconnected block body in RAM until the reorg completes. The code's own comment names this path ("dumptxoutset to an assumeutxo height, invalidateblock on an old hash disconnecting tens of thousands of blocks in one loop"); at mainnet block sizes a 10k-block invalidateblock retains on the order of 10+ GB and OOMs the node mid-reorg. The documented MAX_DISCONNECTED_TX_POOL_BYTES protection is inert.

findings.title: A fork block failing with a non-allowlisted error is neither poisoned nor excluded from candidate selection, so activate-best-chain repeats the same reorg-and-rollback forever and never tries the next-best chain
findings.core_does: ConnectTip failure calls InvalidBlockFound, which sets BLOCK_FAILED_VALID and erases the block from setBlockIndexCandidates for EVERY invalid result except BLOCK_MUTATED. ActivateBestChain then wipes its cached pindexMostWork and re-runs FindMostWorkChain, whose fFailedChain walk removes the whole doomed branch and returns the next-best candidate — so the loop always makes progress.
findings.we_do: %REORG-CONNECT poisons the failing block only for the 8 keywords in *DETERMINISTIC-INVALID-BLOCK-ERRORS* (block.lisp:3004-3013). Anything else (:script-failed, :bad-merkle-root, :too-many-sigops, :bad-witness-merkle-match, :unexpected-witness, :time-too-old, ...) leaves the branch :header-valid with its body on disk. ACTIVATE-BEST-CHAIN's failure arm just stores the keyword in MISSING and returns (3766-3769); BEST-VALID-TIP filters only on `:invalid` + body present, so the next sync pass selects the identical candidate.
findings.impact: Every run-ibd pass (~30 s) disconnects the active chain to the fork point, re-validates fork blocks up to the failing one, and rolls the whole active chain back — indefinitely, with the tip never moving. Worse, since activate-best-chain returns after the single max-work candidate fails, a genuinely valid competing branch that also outweighs the tip is never activated: the node is stuck behind the bad fork. The section comment at block.lisp:2994 claims the cost is bounded by "retry-best-reorg-candidate's bounded rejected-set", but that set (ibd.lisp:3329-3336) is consulted only by %best-completable-reorg-target — activate-best-chain, the driver added later and the one that runs unconditionally every pass, never looks at it. That mitigation reasoning is wrong.

findings.title: No ZMQ block-connected, -blocknotify or fee-estimator block notification for blocks connected through a reorg
findings.our_ref: src/validation/block.lisp:3342-3369 (%reorg-commit connected loop) vs :2656-2665 (connect-block tip-extension arm)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/validation.cpp:3429-3435 (BlockConnected per connected block), :3452-3470 (UpdatedBlockTip + blockTip after each step); refs/bitcoin/src/zmq/zmqnotificationinterface.cpp:150-158, 180-195
findings.core_does: ActivateBestChain fires signals->BlockConnected for every block in connectTrace — reorg-connected blocks included — which drives ZMQ hashtx/rawtx plus the sequence 'C' NotifyBlockConnect; then UpdatedBlockTip fires hashblock/rawblock, and GetNotifications().blockTip drives the block-tip notification, once per step.
findings.we_do: %REORG-COMMIT's connected loop calls index-block-connected, mempool-remove-for-block, orphan-erase-for-block, note-block-connected, wallet-notify-block-connected and the fee-estimator stats — but never `bl:zmq-notify-block-connected`, `bl:notify-block-tip` or `bl.mp:bpe-note-block`. Grep confirms those three have exactly one call site each, all inside connect-block's tip-extension arm (2656, 2662, 2665). The disconnect side DOES notify ZMQ (3330).
findings.impact: On every reorg, ZMQ subscribers (Electrum servers, LND, indexers) receive the 'D' sequence messages for the undone blocks and then nothing at all for the new chain — no hashblock, no rawblock, no 'C', no hashtx for the newly-confirmed transactions. -blocknotify never fires for a reorg either, and the block policy estimator misses every reorg-connected block. Downstream consumers are left believing the chain went backwards and stopped.

findings.title: invalidateblock reorgs only to the invalidated block's parent and never re-activates the best remaining valid chain
findings.core_does: The RPC helper runs InvalidateBlock and then, if the state is valid, calls `chainman.ActiveChainstate().ActivateBestChain(state)` synchronously before returning — so by the time invalidateblock returns, the node has already switched to the best remaining valid chain. (Core's ReconsiderBlock does the same.)
findings.we_do: INVALIDATE-BLOCK performs one PERFORM-REORG from the tip down to the invalidated block's PARENT, marks the subtree :invalid, and returns. It never calls ACTIVATE-BEST-CHAIN. The RPC handler (%chain-control-block) adds nothing. RECONSIDER-BLOCK, by contrast, does re-select via best-valid-tip.
findings.impact: After invalidateblock the node sits on the parent block even when a fully-downloaded competing branch with more work is available. It only recovers when run-ibd's next 30 s pass happens to call activate-best-chain, so the RPC's synchronous contract is broken: the standard operator/functional-test idiom `invalidateblock(h); getbestblockhash() == other_tip` races and usually reports the wrong tip. On a node whose sync thread is not running that pass (e.g. -connect=0 with peers present), the switch may not happen at all.

findings.title: %reorg-commit fires tx-relay and wallet side effects without connect-block's background-chainstate role guard
findings.our_ref: src/validation/block.lisp:3342-3369 (no target-blockhash guard) vs :2676-2699 (connect-block's explicit `(unless (bl.store:chain-state-target-blockhash chain-state) ...)` guard)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/zmq/zmqnotificationinterface.cpp:180-183 (`if (role.historical) return;`), refs/bitcoin/src/validation.cpp:3416, 3429-3435 (ChainstateRole passed to every BlockConnected), :3452 (`this == &m_chainman.ActiveChainstate()` gate on UpdatedBlockTip/blockTip)
findings.core_does: Every BlockConnected carries the ChainstateRole and consumers drop it for the historical/background chainstate; UpdatedBlockTip and the blockTip notification are gated on `this == ActiveChainstate()`. A background chainstate re-deriving pre-snapshot history therefore never touches tx-relay state, the wallet, or the tip notifications.
findings.we_do: CONNECT-BLOCK carries the guard explicitly and cites the Core reason, but the reorg path does not: %REORG-COMMIT calls `note-block-connected` (3367), `wallet-notify-block-connected` (3368), `orphan-erase-for-block` (3365) and `reset-recent-confirmed` (3319) unconditionally, and `readd-disconnected-txs-to-mempool` (3394) works the node's single shared mempool whichever chainstate is being advanced.
findings.impact: If an assumeutxo background chainstate ever reaches PERFORM-REORG (activate-block case 2), ancient blocks would be recorded as the tip-relay 'most recent block', ancient txids would be marked recently-confirmed (suppressing legitimate relay), and the wallet would be told ancient blocks just connected. I could not construct a reachable trigger today — activate-block's target filter plus the in-order historical download keep the background chainstate on the case-1 (extend-tip) path — so this is latent divergence rather than an observed bug, but the guard connect-block deliberately has is simply missing from its sibling.

findings.title: getblocktemplate returns a cached template verbatim — curtime, bits and target are never refreshed, so on min-difficulty chains the served nBits goes stale
findings.our_ref: /Users/sen/common-lisp/bitcoin-lisp/src/rpc/mining.lisp:332-334 (cache hit returns the stored alist) and :336-354 (%gbt-cached-result), with curtime/bits/target frozen at build time in %gbt-assemble :389-397
findings.core_does: Core caches the *template object* only. After the cache decision it always does `CBlock block{block_template->getBlock()}; UpdateTime(&block, consensusParams, pindexPrev); block.nNonce = 0;` (mining.cpp:885-888). UpdateTime sets nTime = max(GetMinimumTime(pindexPrev), now) and, when `consensusParams.fPowAllowMinDifficultyBlocks`, RECOMPUTES `pblock->nBits = GetNextWorkRequired(pindexPrev, pblock, consensusParams)` (miner.cpp:55-62). Only then does it build the reply: hashTarget is derived from the refreshed block.nBits (mining.cpp:939), and curtime/bits come from the refreshed block (mining.cpp:1013-1014). So every getblocktemplate call, cache hit or not, emits a current curtime and a current nBits/target.
findings.we_do: %gbt-build-and-cache stores the finished JSON alist (src/rpc/mining.lisp:356-363) and %gbt-cached-result returns that whole alist unmodified on a hit (:345-354). There is no equivalent of UpdateTime on the cache-hit path: "curtime", "bits" and "target" are whatever assemble-block-template computed when the template was first built (src/mining/assembler.lisp:250-253 computes curtime = max(now, mintime) and bits = next-block-required-bits(tip, curtime) once). The cache is valid while the tip is unchanged AND (mempool counter unchanged OR age <= 5 s), so on a quiet chain it can be reused indefinitely.
findings.impact: On testnet3/testnet4/regtest (fPowAllowMinDifficultyBlocks = true) the required nBits changes purely with wall-clock time: once now > tip_time + 1200 the expected bits become powLimit. Core's next getblocktemplate hands the miner the easy powLimit target; ours keeps serving the pre-20-minute (hard) bits and a stale curtime for as long as the tip and mempool sit still. Two consequences: (a) the miner grinds against a target that is orders of magnitude harder than the chain now requires, so the testnet tip stalls instead of recovering via the min-difficulty rule; (b) "time" is advertised as mutable, so a miner that bumps nTime past tip+1200 while keeping the served bits produces a header our own VALIDATE-DIFFICULTY (src/validation/block.lisp:533-570) rejects as :bad-difficulty. Note getmininginfo's "next" block recomputes bits on every call (src/rpc/mining.lisp:448-453), so the two RPCs of the same node disagree about the next block's difficulty.

findings.title: Block templates never signal any BIP9 deployment: nVersion is the hardcoded constant 0x20000000 and vbavailable is hardcoded empty
findings.core_does: CreateNewBlock sets `pblock->nVersion = m_chainstate.m_chainman.m_versionbitscache.ComputeBlockVersion(pindexPrev, chainparams.GetConsensus())` and, on MineBlocksOnDemand chains, lets `-blockversion=N` override it (miner.cpp:140-145). getblocktemplate then walks `chainman.m_versionbitscache.GBTStatus(*pindexPrev, consensusParams)`: signalling and locked_in deployments are added to `vbavailable` and OR'd into block.nVersion (mining.cpp:958-976), active mandatory rules that the client did not declare throw "Support for '%s' rule requires explicit client support" (mining.cpp:977-983), and the resulting `block.nVersion` is what is emitted (mining.cpp:986).
findings.we_do: block-template-version is the fixed constant +versionbits-top-bits+ = #x20000000 (assembler.lisp:54,72); nothing ever sets it. getblocktemplate emits that constant as "version", a hardcoded empty object for "vbavailable" and 0 for "vbrequired", justified by the comment "No BIP9 deployment is currently pending on any of our networks" (rpc/mining.lisp:413-419). `-blockversion` is in the ignored core-only option list (src/config-options.lisp:391). The versionbits state machine that could answer this exists and is correct (src/validation/versionbits.lisp, incl. the per-chain table at :54-77) but has no caller here — it feeds getdeploymentinfo only.
findings.impact: The comment's reasoning is wrong for regtest: its testdummy deployment has start_time 0 / NO_TIMEOUT (our own table, versionbits.lisp:75, transcribed from chainparams.cpp:580-591), so it is permanently STARTED and Core's regtest template signals bit 28 — mining_basic.py:87 asserts `VERSIONBITS_TOP_BITS + (1 << 28)` and mining_basic.py:83 asserts the `-blockversion=1337` override, both of which we fail. The larger consequence is structural: a pool driven by our getblocktemplate cannot signal for any future BIP9 soft fork, and cannot learn a pending deployment's bit from vbavailable, because the plumbing from the versionbits cache into the template does not exist.

findings.title: generateblock builds its own coinbase and re-introduces the unconditional segwit witness that builder.lisp already fixed
