findings.core_does: generateblock takes the block from CreateNewBlock and then calls RegenerateCommitments(block, chainman) (mining.cpp:389), which drops the old commitment output and calls GenerateCoinbaseCommitment -> UpdateUncommittedBlockStructures. The commitment OUTPUT is added unconditionally (validation.cpp:4033-4049), but the coinbase WITNESS (the 32-byte reserved value) is installed only under `DeploymentActiveAfter(pindexPrev, *this, Consensus::DEPLOYMENT_SEGWIT)` (validation.cpp:4021).
findings.we_do: rpc-generateblock builds the coinbase itself: `(bl.mining:build-coinbase-transaction height subsidy :script-pubkey ... :witness-commitment-script (%witness-commitment-script-for-txs txs))` with no `:segwit-active` argument, so build-coinbase-transaction's default `(segwit-active t)` applies (src/mining/builder.lisp:16) and the reserved witness value is always attached (builder.lisp:63-67). The shared path, assemble-full-block, passes the correct gate `(>= height (bl.val:get-segwit-activation-height bl:*network*))` (builder.lisp:110-114) — a fix whose docstring (builder.lisp:23-38) documents this exact bug — but that fix never reached this second construction site.
findings.impact: On a chain where segwit is not yet active (we do support `-testactivationheight=segwit@N`, src/config-options.lisp:128 and src/validation/block.lisp:178-252), generateblock produces a coinbase carrying witness data below height N. Our contextual validation rejects that as :unexpected-witness, so the TestBlockValidity dry run at src/rpc/mining.lisp:773-778 fails and the RPC errors with -25 for every call; Core's generateblock succeeds on the same chain. It also means the two coinbase-construction sites can drift again on any future change.

findings.title: getnetworkhashps computes the wrong number: integer rounding drops sub-1 H/s results to 0, and the timespan uses the window's endpoints instead of its min/max block time
findings.core_does: Core walks the window block by block accumulating `minTime = min(time, minTime)` and `maxTime = max(time, maxTime)` (mining.cpp:91-99), returns 0 when minTime == maxTime (mining.cpp:102-103), and returns `workDiff.getdouble() / timeDiff` — a double (mining.cpp:105-108).
findings.we_do: `dtime` is `tip.header.timestamp - start.header.timestamp` — only the two endpoints — and the result is `(round dwork dtime)`, which yields an INTEGER (src/rpc/mining.lisp:813-819).
findings.impact: Any hash rate below 0.5 H/s reports as 0 and every larger value is truncated to whole hashes/second. On regtest the true value is 1/300 = 0.00333; we return 0, while mining_basic.py:399 asserts `round(mining_info['networkhashps'], 5) == Decimal('0.00333')` and rpc_blockchain.py:535-536 asserts `abs(hps*300 - 1) < 0.0001`. Separately, because block timestamps are not monotonic, the endpoint-difference timespan can be smaller than (or negative where Core's max-min is positive) the real span, inflating or zeroing the estimate on a real chain; ours returns 0 for a non-increasing endpoint pair where Core returns a finite rate.

findings.title: getnetworkhashps ignores its `height` argument entirely, does not implement nblocks = -1, and never validates its inputs
findings.core_does: GetNetworkHashPS(lookup, height, chain) throws RPC_INVALID_PARAMETER "Invalid nblocks. Must be a positive number or -1." when `lookup < -1 || lookup == 0` (mining.cpp:66-68); throws "Block does not exist at specified height" when `height < -1 || height > active_chain.Height()` (mining.cpp:70-72); anchors the window at `active_chain[height]` when height >= 0 (mining.cpp:74-78), returning 0 at genesis; and expands lookup == -1 to `pb->nHeight % DifficultyAdjustmentInterval() + 1`, i.e. blocks since the last difficulty change (mining.cpp:83-85).
findings.we_do: `(let ((n (first params))) (if (and (integerp n) (> n 0)) n 120))` — anything that is not a positive integer (0, -1, -100, a string) silently becomes 120; the second parameter is never read at all, and the window is always anchored at the current tip (src/rpc/mining.lisp:802-806).
findings.impact: `getnetworkhashps(100, 0)` returns the tip-window estimate instead of 0 (genesis); `getnetworkhashps(100, <past height>)` silently answers about the tip instead of that height — a wrong answer with no error, which is the worst failure mode for a monitoring caller. `getnetworkhashps(-1)` returns the 120-block average instead of the since-last-retarget average, and `getnetworkhashps(0)` / `(-100)` / `("a", [])` return a number where Core raises -8 / -3. rpc_blockchain.py:496-547 exercises every one of these.

findings.title: getmininginfo reports currentblockweight/currentblocktx as 0 before any template has been assembled; Core omits the fields
findings.core_does: `m_last_block_num_txs` and `m_last_block_weight` are `std::optional<int64_t>` (miner.h:95-99) and getmininginfo pushes each key only `if (BlockAssembler::m_last_block_*)` (mining.cpp:466-467), so a node that has never assembled a template omits both keys. The RPC result declaration marks them `/*optional=*/true` with "only present if a block was ever assembled".
findings.we_do: `("currentblockweight" . (if template ... 0))` and `("currentblocktx" . (if template ... 0))` — the keys are always present, with 0 standing in for "never assembled" (src/rpc/mining.lisp:456-457).
findings.impact: A caller cannot distinguish "no template has ever been built" from "the last template was empty and weighed 0" — and 0 is not even a reachable weight, since Core's counter always includes the reserved weight (8000 by default). mining_basic.py:388-389 asserts `'currentblocktx' not in mining_info` and `'currentblockweight' not in mining_info` on a node that has only used generate*; our reply carries both keys.

findings.title: generatetoaddress / generatetodescriptor raise an error when maxtries is exhausted instead of returning the blocks mined so far
findings.core_does: GenerateBlock grinds `while (max_tries > 0 && nNonce < UINT32_MAX && !CheckProofOfWork(...) && !chainman.m_interrupt)` and returns FALSE when max_tries hits 0 or the node is interrupting (mining.cpp:142-148). generateBlocks treats that as `break` and returns the UniValue array accumulated so far, which may be shorter than nGenerate or empty (mining.cpp:167-181). max_tries is shared across the whole nblocks loop, and the interrupt check makes the grind abortable at shutdown.
findings.we_do: `(unless (bl.mining:mine-block block :max-tries maxtries) (error 'rpc-error :code +rpc-misc-error+ :message "Failed to find a valid nonce"))` (src/rpc/mining.lisp:624-625). maxtries is applied afresh to each of the nblocks iterations rather than being a shared budget, and mine-block's `dotimes` (builder.lisp:127-132) has no interrupt check.
findings.impact: A caller that deliberately bounds the work — `generatetoaddress(1, addr, 0)` or a small maxtries on a real-difficulty chain — gets an RPC error from us where Core returns `[]` (or a partial list) as a normal result, and any blocks already mined in earlier loop iterations are discarded from the reply. On a non-regtest chain the un-interruptible grind also keeps an RPC worker thread busy through shutdown, where Core's loop exits on chainman.m_interrupt.

findings.title: The BIP94 timewarp floor and check use the fixed 2016-block interval and a hardcoded testnet4 gate; the comment justifying this misreads Core
findings.core_does: GetMinimumTime takes `difficulty_adjustment_interval` as a parameter and applies the `pindexPrev->GetBlockTime() - MAX_TIMEWARP` floor on EVERY network at `height % interval == 0` — the comment is explicit: "Account for BIP94 timewarp rule on all networks. This makes future activation safer" (miner.cpp:41-45). The interval is `nPowTargetTimespan / nPowTargetSpacing`, which is 144 on regtest (86400/600, chainparams.cpp:576-577) and 2016 elsewhere. The consensus check is gated on `consensusParams.enforce_BIP94` (validation.cpp:4129), true on testnet4 and on regtest whenever `-test=bip94` is given (chainparams.cpp:47, kernel/chainparams.cpp:579).
findings.we_do: next-block-mintime applies the clamp at `(zerop (mod height bl.store:+difficulty-adjustment-interval+))` with the fixed constant 2016 for every network (assembler.lisp:89-95), and bip94-timewarp-violation-p is gated on `(eq bl:*network* :testnet4)` with the same fixed 2016 (block.lisp:637-639). The assembler comment defends this as "matches every network except regtest (Core: 144), where BIP94 is off and the extra floor is moot".
findings.impact: The comment's reasoning is wrong on both halves. (a) Core's template floor is not conditioned on enforce_BIP94 at all, so on regtest Core raises mintime at every multiple of 144 and we raise it at multiples of 2016 — our templates offer a mintime Core would not. (b) regtest CAN enforce BIP94 in consensus via `-test=bip94`; our validation cannot, because the check is hardcoded to testnet4 and to a 2016 interval. mining_basic.py:193-247 runs exactly this scenario (`-test=bip94`, DIFFICULTY_ADJUSTMENT_INTERVAL = 144) and asserts both the clamped `tmpl['curtime'] == tmpl['mintime']` and a -25 'time-timewarp-attack' from submitheader; we would clamp at the wrong heights and accept the timewarped header.

findings.title: cmpctblock has no anti-DoS work threshold, and the anti-replay gate only fires for headers already in the index — every replay rebuilds the whole-mempool short-ID map
findings.core_does: Before doing ANY work on a compact block, Core checks `prev_block->nChainWork + GetBlockProof(cmpctblock.header) < GetAntiDoSWorkThreshold()` and returns (net_processing.cpp:4578-4582, "Ignoring low-work compact block"). It then runs ProcessNewBlockHeaders so the header IS in the index, and only then reaches the second gate `pindex->nChainWork <= ActiveChain().Tip()->nChainWork || pindex->nTx != 0` -> return (:4645-4655), plus `!already_in_flight && !CanDirectFetch()` -> return (:4657-4659) and `pindex->nHeight <= ActiveChain().Height() + 2` (:4661). PartiallyDownloadedBlock::InitData (the mempool short-ID pass) is only reached past all four.
findings.we_do: COMPACT-BLOCK-HEADER-VERDICT (protocol.lisp:3467-3573) has no work threshold at all — ANTI-DOS-WORK-THRESHOLD exists (src/networking/headers-sync.lisp:377) but is used only by MAYBE-START-PRESYNC (headers-sync.lisp:414), never here. The only work comparison is inside the `(and known ...)` arm at :3515, i.e. it applies solely to a header ALREADY in our block index. Our cmpctblock path never inserts the header (the function is pure reads; the header is indexed only by ACCEPT-DOWNLOADED-BLOCK after a *complete* reconstruction), so for a header we have not seen KNOWN is NIL, we fall to the `(t ...)` arm, VALIDATE-BLOCK-HEADER (src/validation/block.lisp:655) passes on PoW/MTP/bits alone with no minimum-chain-work or checkpoint test, the verdict is :ACCEPT, and HANDLE-CMPCTBLOCK calls RECONSTRUCT-COMPACT-BLOCK (:3654) -> BUILD-SHORTID-MAP (:3266), which does `maphash` over the ENTIRE mempool (src/mempool/mempool.lisp:1861), one SipHash + one cons + one hash-table insert per entry, into a freshly allocated table. The reconstruction then fails with missing indexes, so the header is still never indexed and the identical message can be replayed forever. "cmpctblock" also has no bucket in CHECK-PEER-RATE-LIMIT (src/networking/peer.lisp:1828-1841 falls through to `(t nil)` = unlimited). The code comment at :3502-3514 names this exact attack ("a peer can replay one cmpctblock forever and make us hash the WHOLE MEMPOOL into a shortid map each time") but the guard it introduces is gated on KNOWN, which the attack case never satisfies.
findings.impact: Any peer, inbound or outbound, that once mines a single valid-PoW header on top of an ancient low-difficulty block (mainnet height 1-2 requires ~2^32 hashes at bits 0x1d00ffff — seconds on a GPU; on testnet3/testnet4 the 20-minute min-difficulty rule makes it free at the tip) can replay that ~130-byte cmpctblock indefinitely. Each message costs a full mempool SipHash pass plus a fresh N-entry hash table that becomes garbage. The pump grants 32 messages per peer per ~1 s cycle on the same thread that runs block validation, so with a 50k-entry mempool one connection buys roughly 0.2-0.3 s of CPU and ~50 MB of garbage per second, and N connections multiply it. No misbehaviour is recorded on this path (the verdict is :ACCEPT), no rate limit applies, and the node's single sync thread stops following the tip.

findings.title: We never push an unsolicited cmpctblock to peers that selected us as their BIP152 high-bandwidth peer
findings.core_does: Core pushes CMPCTBLOCK on its own initiative in two places, both driven by `state.m_requested_hb_cmpctblocks`: NewPoWValidBlock (net_processing.cpp:2144-2152) sends header-and-ids the moment a block with valid PoW arrives and the peer has the parent, and SendMessages (:5893-5910) sends the cached m_most_recent_compact_block instead of a headers announcement when exactly one block is to be announced. That push is the entire point of BIP152 high-bandwidth mode.
findings.we_do: RELAY-BLOCK (protocol.lisp:3053-3072) is our only outbound block-announcement path and it emits only a `headers` message (BIP130 peers) or an `inv` — there is no cmpctblock branch. `grep make-cmpctblock-message src/` returns exactly two sites: HANDLE-GETDATA's MSG_CMPCT_BLOCK responder (protocol.lisp:2132) and the cache builder (src/validation/block.lisp:2449). We do record the peer's request — HANDLE-SENDCMPCT sets PEER-COMPACT-BLOCK-HIGH-BANDWIDTH (protocol.lisp:3260, Core's m_bip152_highbandwidth_from) — and report it through getpeerinfo `bip152_hb_from` (src/rpc/net.lisp:247), but nothing ever reads it to drive a send.
findings.impact: Every peer that selects us as one of its three high-bandwidth compact-block sources gets a headers/inv announcement instead of the block, so it must issue a getdata and wait a full round trip for data it asked us to push. Our node is a systematically slower relay hop than any Core node for exactly the peers that chose us to be fast, and getpeerinfo advertises an HB relationship we do not honour. It also wastes the m_most_recent_compact_block cache we already maintain.

findings.title: sendcmpct(0) never clears the recorded high-bandwidth-from flag
findings.core_does: `nodestate->m_requested_hb_cmpctblocks = sendcmpct_hb; pfrom.m_bip152_highbandwidth_from = sendcmpct_hb;` — an unconditional assignment, so sendcmpct(0,2) demotes the peer back to low bandwidth exactly as sendcmpct(1,2) promotes it (net_processing.cpp:3917-3919).
findings.we_do: HANDLE-SENDCMPCT writes the flag only in the true direction: `(when high-bandwidth (setf (peer-compact-block-high-bandwidth peer) t))` (protocol.lisp:3259-3260). Once set, a later sendcmpct(0,2) from the same peer leaves it T for the life of the connection.
findings.impact: Today the consequence is confined to getpeerinfo's `bip152_hb_from`, which keeps reporting T after the peer demoted us — a misleading operator/diagnostic signal. It becomes a live relay bug the moment the missing HB push (finding above) is implemented, because we would keep pushing unsolicited compact blocks to a peer that explicitly asked us to stop.

findings.title: Gossiped addresses are stored in addrman and relayed onward without the banned/discouraged filter Core applies at ingest
findings.core_does: In the per-address loop of the ADDR/ADDRV2 handler, after AddAddressKnown, Core does `if (m_banman && (m_banman->IsDiscouraged(addr) || m_banman->IsBanned(addr))) continue;` with the comment "Do not process banned/discouraged addresses beyond remembering we received them" (net_processing.cpp:4093-4097). The `continue` skips BOTH the RelayAddress call (:4101-4104) and the vAddrOk push that feeds m_addrman.Add (:4106-4108).
findings.we_do: %INGEST-GOSSIPED-ADDRESS (protocol.lisp:1208-1259) filters on MAY-HAVE-USEFUL-ADDRESS-DB-P and REACHABLE-NETWORK-P only; it calls ADDRESS-BOOK-ADD at :1250 and returns a relay candidate at :1254-1259 with no ban/discourage test. `grep -rn 'peer-discouraged-p|peer-banned-p' src/` shows our only filter sites are %SAMPLE-ADDR-RESPONSE (protocol.lisp:2487, getaddr response fill) and CONNECT-PEER (peer.lisp:300, dial time) — neither is the ingest path.
findings.impact: Banned and discouraged addresses occupy addrman buckets, evicting good entries, and — more visibly — we gossip them onward to up to two peers each, so our node actively re-propagates addresses it has itself decided are hostile. The getaddr-response filter mitigates only the pull path, not RELAY-ADDRESS.

findings.title: Relayed addresses go out immediately, one addr message per address, instead of Core's per-peer Poisson-batched queue
findings.core_does: RelayAddress calls PushAddress, which only appends to `peer.m_addrs_to_send`. MaybeSendAddr flushes the whole accumulated vector as ONE addr/addrv2 message, and only once `current_time > peer.m_next_addr_send`, where that deadline is re-drawn as `rand_exp_duration(AVG_ADDRESS_BROADCAST_INTERVAL)` with AVG_ADDRESS_BROADCAST_INTERVAL = 30 s (net_processing.cpp:160, 5571-5597).
findings.we_do: RELAY-ADDRESS builds a one-address addr/addrv2 message per target and calls SEND-MESSAGE synchronously inside the announcement loop (protocol.lisp:1153-1159), from the ADDR handler's own call site (%PROCESS-GOSSIPED-ADDRESSES, protocol.lisp:1338-1340). There is no per-peer m_addrs_to_send equivalent and no send timer; the per-peer known-addrs bloom filter is the only batching-adjacent state.
findings.impact: The exponential send timer is Core's defence against timing correlation: a peer receiving our gossip learns, to within milliseconds, when we received that address from someone else, which helps map who is connected to whom. Emitting one message per address also multiplies message count (an addr carrying 10 relayable addresses produces up to 20 outgoing messages instead of 2 batched ones) and burns framing overhead on every hop.

findings.title: wtxidrelay / sendaddrv2 received after VERACK are silently ignored where Core disconnects
findings.core_does: Both arms begin with `if (pfrom.fSuccessfullyConnected) { LogDebug(... "received after verack"); pfrom.fDisconnect = true; return; }` — WTXIDRELAY at net_processing.cpp:3927-3934 and SENDADDRV2 at :3949-3956. BIP155/BIP339 require the negotiation to sit between VERSION and VERACK, and Core enforces it by dropping the connection.
findings.we_do: HANDLE-MESSAGE treats both as inert post-handshake no-ops returning T (protocol.lisp:257-264, "No-op post-handshake (only meaningful during handshake)"). The neighbouring sendtxrcncl comment at :268-273 states these two are no-ops in Core "unlike the sendaddrv2/wtxidrelay no-op stubs above" — that reading of Core is wrong; Core disconnects on all three.
findings.impact: Missing hardening rather than a live bug: because we also ignore the flag rather than flipping relay mode mid-connection, no relay state actually changes. But a peer can spam these post-verack at zero cost with no penalty, and p2p_handshake.py-style parity tests that assert the disconnect will fail against us.

findings.title: A backed-up send buffer makes us DROP outbound messages; Core instead stops processing inbound messages until it drains
findings.core_does: ProcessMessages returns false before polling a new message when `node.fPauseSend` is set (net_processing.cpp:5244-5245), and ProcessGetData breaks out of the loop on the same flag (:2536) leaving the rest of the request queued in peer.m_getdata_requests (:2558). Nothing Core has already decided to send is ever discarded — the work is deferred until the socket drains.
findings.we_do: SEND-BYTES returns NIL and DISCARDS the message once `connection-send-queue-bytes` exceeds +max-send-buffer-bytes+ (1,000,000; src/networking/connection.lisp:451-456, 493-497). The drain loop in DRAIN-AND-REAP-PEER (src/networking/ibd.lisp:1784-1813) keeps reading and dispatching regardless of send pause; only HANDLE-GETDATA (protocol.lisp:1988-1991) and HANDLE-GETBLOCKTXN (protocol.lisp:2306) consult CONNECTION-SEND-PAUSED-P.
findings.impact: While we are streaming a large block to a slow peer, our replies to that peer's other requests are silently dropped rather than deferred: a getheaders answer, a pong, a tx we just invd. Nothing retries most of those, so the peer waits forever on a request we already consumed, and a dropped pong can make an otherwise healthy peer disconnect us on its own ping timeout. Core's design never loses a message because it stops consuming input instead.

findings.title: Transaction deserializer accepts the BIP144 extended encoding with all-empty witness stacks; Core throws "Superfluous witness record"
findings.our_ref: src/serialization/types.lisp:209-232 (br-read-transaction); same gap in read-transaction at src/serialization/types.lisp:266-289
findings.core_does: UnserializeTransaction reads the witness stacks for every vin and then does `if (!tx.HasWitness()) throw std::ios_base::failure("Superfluous witness record");` (transaction.h:229-230). A transaction serialized as version|00|01|vin|vout|<all-empty stacks>|locktime is therefore UNDESERIALIZABLE in Core — the tx message, and any block containing such a transaction, fails to parse and is never accepted.
findings.we_do: br-read-transaction checks only that the flag byte equals 1 (types.lisp:219-220), reads input-count witness stacks (types.lisp:225-226) and returns the transaction with no emptiness check. transaction-has-witness-p then reports NIL (types.lisp:169-173), so the tx behaves as a legacy transaction: txid, wtxid, weight and merkle root are all computed from the legacy re-serialization and are self-consistent. Nothing in parse-tx-payload (messages.lisp:441-457, which only checks for trailing bytes), br-read-bitcoin-block (types.lisp:563-569) or block validation rejects it. Grep for "Superfluous" across src/ finds the string only in comments on the SERIALIZE side (types.lisp:422, rpc/mining.lisp:52) — the decoder has no such guard.
findings.impact: A miner can produce a block whose bytes every Core node rejects as malformed while we accept it and build on it. We follow a chain the rest of the network will not, until a reorg. The same encoding also lets a peer put into our mempool a transaction Core cannot parse at all. Note the asymmetry that makes this easy to miss: because we re-serialize the block in normalized (legacy) form for disk and for relay, the block hash is unchanged, so the divergence is invisible in our own logs and only shows up as "Core peers rejected the block we accepted".

findings.title: Lax (pre-BIP66) DER signature parser diverges from Core's ecdsa_signature_parse_der_lax in both directions
findings.core_does: Core's lax parser supports long-form DER length descriptors for the R and S INTEGERs (pubkey.cpp:84-106 for R, 119-145 for S: `lenbyte = input[pos++]; if (lenbyte & 0x80) { ... accumulate rlen ... }`), and on an integer that is longer than 32 bytes after leading zeros are stripped it sets `overflow = 1` (pubkey.cpp:157-159, 169-171) and substitutes an all-zero signature, so verification is guaranteed to FAIL. The header comment (pubkey.cpp:35-43) states the parser is known to support every format violation present in the chain before BIP66.
findings.we_do: parse-der-integer-lax reads the length byte as a plain short-form value with no long-form branch (secp256k1.lisp:435-437), so `02 81 20 <32 bytes>` is read as len=0x81=129 and the whole signature is rejected. In the other direction, normalize-signature-lax converts R and S to bignums and then calls integer-to-bytes-be with byte-count 32 (secp256k1.lisp:454-460, 487-488), which SILENTLY TRUNCATES to the low 32 bytes instead of failing — so R encoded as `02 21 01 <r 32 bytes>` (= 2^256 + r) collapses back to r and the signature verifies.
findings.impact: Only reachable while DERSIG is off, i.e. blocks below the BIP66 activation height (src/validation/block.lisp:322-323 gates DERSIG on get-bip66-activation-height), so no live mainnet split. But it is a two-way consensus divergence on historical validation: (a) a pre-BIP66 signature using a long-form integer length makes CHECKSIG false for us and true for Core — we would reject a block the network considers valid and IBD stalls permanently at that height; (b) an inflated >32-byte R/S makes CHECKSIG true for us and false for Core, so we accept a spend Core rejects. Reachable on regtest below height 1351 and testnet3 below 330,776 as well.

findings.title: Coinbase "hash" (wtxid) reported as 32 zero bytes by the RPC transaction serializer; Core reports the real witness hash
findings.core_does: CTransaction::ComputeWitnessHash has no coinbase special case — it returns the txid when the tx has no witness and otherwise hash256 of the witness serialization. The all-zero value is applied ONLY inside BlockWitnessMerkleRoot (merkle.cpp:80, `leaves.emplace_back(); // The witness hash of the coinbase is 0`), never in the transaction's own identity. So getblock verbosity 2/3 and getrawtransaction report the coinbase's true witness hash.
findings.we_do: transaction-wtxid special-cases any transaction whose first input is a null outpoint and returns 32 zero bytes (types.lisp:443-446), and tx-to-json feeds that straight into the "hash" field (blockchain.lisp:466). The tree already knows this is wrong — src/wallet/wallet-tx.lisp:87-96 defines %tx-witness-hash precisely to work around it ("Core's GetWitnessHash reports the actual hash") — but only the wallet path uses the workaround; the general RPC path does not.
findings.impact: getblock verbosity 2/3 and getrawtransaction verbose report hash=0000…0000 for the coinbase of every block. Any explorer, indexer or Core functional test that reads or cross-checks the coinbase wtxid sees wrong data. The consensus use of the zero convention (compute-witness-merkle-root, validation/block.lisp:1094) is correct and unaffected.

findings.title: PSBT parser omits two of Core's global-map validity checks (out-of-range prevout index, unsupported PSBT version)
findings.core_does: After matching the non_witness_utxo's txid, Core also requires the outpoint's index to exist in it: `if (tx->vin[i].prevout.n >= input.non_witness_utxo->vout.size()) throw std::ios_base::failure("Input specifies output index that does not exist");` (psbt.h:1375-1377). Separately, a global PSBT_GLOBAL_VERSION greater than PSBT_HIGHEST_VERSION (= 0, psbt.h:80) is rejected with "Unsupported version number" (psbt.h:1322-1323).
findings.we_do: %psbt-validate-input checks only that the non_witness_utxo deserializes, has no trailing bytes, and hashes to the outpoint's txid (psbt.lisp:188-195) — the prevout index is never bounds-checked. parse-psbt checks that the version record is 4 bytes (psbt.lisp:214-215) but never inspects its value, so a v2 PSBT that also carries a global unsigned tx is accepted and processed as v0.
findings.impact: A PSBT that Core refuses to decode is accepted by decodepsbt / analyzepsbt / walletprocesspsbt. For the index case the consumer at src/wallet/psbt.lisp:230-234 bounds-checks and then FALLS BACK to the unauthenticated witness_utxo — which is exactly the fabricated-fee path the comment at src/wallet/psbt.lisp:214-222 was written to close, so the missing parse-time check quietly reopens the fallback it relies on.

findings.title: base58-decode has no length bound; Core's DecodeBase58 bails as soon as the decoded length exceeds max_ret_len
findings.our_ref: src/crypto/address.lisp:43-68 (base58-decode), reached from base58check-decode:85, decode-address:337, bip32-parse:179, wif-to-private-key:120
findings.core_does: DecodeBase58 takes a max_ret_len and aborts inside the per-character loop the moment the accumulated output would exceed it (base58.cpp:50 for leading '1's, base58.cpp:71 `if (length + zeroes > max_ret_len) return false;`). Every call site passes a small bound: 21 bytes for destinations (key_io.cpp:93), 34 for WIF, 78 for extended keys. Core also deliberately skips leading and trailing whitespace (base58.cpp:42-43, and the trailing skip before the NUL check).
findings.we_do: base58-decode accumulates `num = num*58 + digit` over the entire string with no length cap (address.lisp:53-58), producing O(n^2) bignum work before any caller gets to check the result's length. It also rejects whitespace outright, since the space character is not in the decode map.
findings.impact: An RPC or web-UI caller that can pass an arbitrarily long base58 string (validateaddress, getaddressinfo, importdescriptors, any address argument) burns quadratic CPU on the handler thread before the length is ever examined — Core returns immediately. Separately, an address string with surrounding whitespace is accepted by Core and rejected by us, so identical input decodes differently on the two implementations. Authenticated surface only, hence S3.

findings.title: Block bodies are written to disk with no CheckBlock at all on the two IBD persist paths, and a present-but-invalid body is never re-requested
findings.our_ref: src/networking/ibd.lisp:3858-3862 (out-of-order persist), src/networking/ibd.lisp:3644-3649 (competing-fork persist), src/validation/block.lisp:4102-4110 (activate-block case 3)
findings.core_does: AcceptBlock runs the anti-DoS gate (fAlreadyHave / fRequested / fHasMoreOrSameWork / fTooFarAhead / MinimumChainWork, validation.cpp:4367-4378) and THEN `if (!CheckBlock(block, state, params.GetConsensus()) || !ContextualCheckBlock(block, state, *this, pindex->pprev))` before it ever calls m_blockman.WriteBlock. A body whose merkle root does not match its header, or whose first tx is not a coinbase, or that violates CheckTransaction, is refused and InvalidBlockFound is consulted; nothing reaches disk.
findings.we_do: process-received-block dispatches on height. Only the height == tip+1 arm validates (via activate-block case 1). The `height > tip+1` arm calls %out-of-order-block-acceptable-p -- which ports ONLY Core's anti-DoS gate, and its own docstring cites validation.cpp:4367-4378, i.e. the lines just above the CheckBlock it does not port -- and then calls bl.store:store-block directly. The `height <= tip` (competing fork) arm calls store-block with no gate and no validation whatsoever. activate-block's case 3 (weaker/equal chain) does the same. The only body-level test on any of these paths is block-witness-stripped-p. No merkle root, no coinbase structure, no CheckTransaction, no size/weight, no sigop budget.
findings.impact: Any peer that serves a block we requested can substitute an arbitrary transaction list under a valid header. During IBD nearly every arriving block takes the out-of-order arm (we request a window ahead of the tip), and `requested` is true, so it is persisted unvalidated. The body then becomes permanent: the download walk skips any hash for which block-exists-p is true (src/networking/ibd.lisp:1130), queue-missing-fork-blocks only re-queues bodies that are absent (src/networking/ibd.lisp:3382), and get-block prunes only bodies that fail to DESERIALIZE (src/storage/blocks.lisp:427-440) -- a wrong-merkle-root body parses fine. So one malformed-but-parseable block message wedges the node's sync at a chosen height with no recovery short of manual datadir surgery. Secondary: store-block appends a fresh flat record on every re-store with no already-have check, and the competing-fork arm has no requested/more-work gate, so replaying one fork block body grows blk files without bound while block-store-total-bytes (the pruning accountant) subtracts the old size and under-reports.

findings.title: BIP30 is skipped for essentially the whole chain on testnet4/signet/regtest, where Core enforces it at every height
findings.core_does: `CBlockIndex* pindexBIP34height = pindex->pprev->GetAncestor(params.GetConsensus().BIP34Height); fEnforceBIP30 = fEnforceBIP30 && (!pindexBIP34height || !(pindexBIP34height->GetBlockHash() == params.GetConsensus().BIP34Hash)); if (fEnforceBIP30 || pindex->nHeight >= BIP34_IMPLIES_BIP30_LIMIT) {...}`. On testnet4, signet and regtest, kernel/chainparams.cpp:327-328, :479-480 and :568-569 set BIP34Height = 1 and BIP34Hash = uint256{} (the NULL hash), so the hash can never match a real block and fEnforceBIP30 stays true for every block on those chains. On mainnet/testnet3 the ancestor is null whenever pprev->nHeight < BIP34Height, i.e. Core enforces for every height <= BIP34Height inclusive.
findings.we_do: `(or (and (not (bip30-repeat-block-p height)) (< height (get-bip34-activation-height bl:*network*))) (>= height +bip34-implies-bip30-limit+))`. The BIP34Hash half of Core's condition is dropped entirely and replaced by a strict `<` height comparison, so on testnet4/signet/regtest (bip34-height = 1, src/util/chainparams.lisp:212/248/283) BIP30 runs only at height 0 and again from 1,983,702. On mainnet it also turns off one block early, at height 227,931 itself.
findings.impact: Every block Core rejects with bad-txns-BIP30 on testnet4, signet or regtest we accept, and apply-block-to-utxo-set overwrites the still-unspent coins of the duplicated txid (CVE-2012-1909) -- a consensus split plus silent destruction of UTXOs. It is directly constructible on regtest: -testactivationheight=bip34@N (which we honour, src/validation/block.lisp:1199-1201) leaves pre-N coinbases unconstrained, so a pre-N coinbase can carry the scriptSig prefix of a later height and be replayed verbatim at that height; Core still enforces BIP30 there because BIP34Hash is null, we do not. The docstring's stated justification -- 'omitting only the extra enforcement Core applies on a non-canonical fork past the BIP 34 height' -- is wrong: on three of our five networks the omitted clause is the one that keeps BIP30 on for the whole chain, not a fork-only extra.

findings.title: ContextualCheckBlock's UTXO-free half (finality, BIP34 height, witness malleation, block weight) is deferred to reorg time for every non-tip block
findings.core_does: ContextualCheckBlock takes only `pindexPrev` -- no coins view exists at that point. It runs IsFinalTx over every tx against nHeight and pindexPrev->GetMedianTimePast(), the BIP34 serialized-height prefix, CheckWitnessMalleation, and GetBlockWeight > MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT. It is called on EVERY accepted block, side branches included, before the body is written, and a failure marks the index entry BLOCK_FAILED_VALID.
findings.we_do: validate-block's CONTEXT-FREE-ONLY arm stops after %check-block, and all four of those rules live in %contextual-check-block, which accept-downloaded-block only reaches for a tip-extending block. %contextual-check-block's docstring justifies the grouping with 'Every check here reads the ACTIVE UTXO set or the chain height, so it is only correct for a block that extends the tip' -- but finality needs only the block height and the parent's MTP, BIP34 needs only the height, and CheckWitnessMalleation and the weight check need nothing at all; all four are computable from the fork parent, which is exactly why Core puts them in ContextualCheckBlock rather than ConnectBlock.
findings.impact: A side-branch block that is unconditionally invalid -- non-final transactions, wrong BIP34 coinbase height, unexpected witness data, over-weight -- is accepted and persisted by us, where Core refuses it and permanently marks it invalid. It is then re-read, re-deserialized and re-validated on every reorg attempt that touches that branch, and several of those verdicts (:unexpected-witness, :bad-coinbase-height as reached via reorg) drive the reject/candidate machinery instead of being settled once at admission. Cheap unmetered work for a peer, and it widens the window in which finding 1's corrupt bodies live on disk.

findings.title: Block script validation never consults the script-execution cache, so every mempool-verified transaction is re-interpreted at connect
findings.our_ref: src/validation/block.lisp:793-849 (validate-tx-scripts) vs src/validation/transaction.lisp:1364-1401 (validate-transaction-scripts, which does use it)
findings.core_does: CheckInputScripts hashes (tx.GetWitnessHash(), flags) into hashCacheEntry and returns true immediately on `m_script_execution_cache.contains(...)`. ConnectBlock calls CheckInputScripts for every non-coinbase tx with `fCacheResults = fJustCheck`; the comment there is explicit -- "Don't cache results if we're actually connecting blocks (still consult the cache, though)" -- so a transaction already fully verified during mempool acceptance costs one cache probe at block connect.
findings.we_do: validate-block-scripts dispatches to validate-tx-scripts, which goes straight to collect-spent-utxos + validate-input-script per input with no cache probe and no store. The cache exists and is keyed identically -- (wtxid, flag string) in validate-transaction-scripts -- but only the mempool path reaches it, so its own docstring claim ('the mempool verifies on acceptance and the confirming block verifies again, so this turns the second pass into ONE lookup') never holds.
findings.impact: Every block re-runs the full script interpreter over every input that the mempool already verified under the same flags. The per-signature cache absorbs the ECDSA cost, so this is interpreter and sighash work rather than crypto, but it is thousands of redundant script executions per block at the tip and across the whole of IBD's post-assumevalid range -- pure latency Core does not pay.

findings.title: The intra-block coin overlay keeps provably-unspendable outputs that Core's AddCoin drops
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/coins.cpp AddCoin (`if (coin.out.scriptPubKey.IsUnspendable()) return;`), reached from UpdateCoins in refs/bitcoin/src/validation.cpp:2589
findings.core_does: UpdateCoins -> AddCoins -> AddCoin drops any output whose scriptPubKey IsUnspendable (leading OP_RETURN, or size > MAX_SCRIPT_SIZE). A later transaction in the same block that names such an outpoint fails HaveInputs and the block is rejected bad-txns-inputs-missingorspent by CheckTxInputs.
findings.we_do: %contextual-check-block stages every output of every transaction into pending-utxos with no script-unspendable-p filter, even though apply-block-to-utxo-set (src/storage/coins-view-cache.lisp:786) applies exactly that filter when the block is finally connected. A same-block spend of an OP_RETURN or oversize-script output therefore resolves as a present input here.
findings.impact: The block is still rejected in the normal case, but with the wrong verdict (:script-failed from the OP_RETURN execution instead of :missing-input) and after full script work rather than at the input-availability check. When script checks are skipped (assumevalid ancestors, skip-scripts) nothing catches it at all: the spend is accepted, its value is credited into total-fees, and the coinbase cap is raised by an amount Core never grants.

findings.title: CheckTxInputs' input-value MoneyRange guards and ConnectBlock's accumulated-fee guard have no analogue
findings.core_does: CheckTxInputs rejects bad-txns-inputvalues-outofrange when `!MoneyRange(coin.out.nValue) || !MoneyRange(nValueIn)` and bad-txns-fee-outofrange when the derived fee leaves range; ConnectBlock separately rejects bad-txns-accumulated-fee-outofrange when the running nFees sum leaves MoneyRange.
findings.we_do: validate-transaction-contextual sums input values into a Satoshi (an unbounded Coalton Integer, src/coalton/types.lisp:74-77) with no per-coin or running range check, and %contextual-check-block accumulates total-fees with satoshi+ and never range-checks it before computing max-coinbase-value.
findings.impact: No overflow is possible for us because the amounts are bignums, so this cannot be exploited on a chain whose supply is bounded by consensus. It is a missing defence-in-depth layer rather than a live bug: any path that seeds the coins view from outside block validation (a UTXO snapshot, a corrupted chainstate record) hands an out-of-range coin value straight into the fee sum and thence into the coinbase cap, where Core would have refused it.

findings.title: enforce_BIP94 is hardcoded to testnet4; Core lets regtest turn it on with -test=bip94
findings.core_does: Regtest sets `consensus.enforce_BIP94 = opts.enforce_bip94`, and chainparams.cpp:47 sets that from `HasTestOption(args, "bip94")`. ContextualCheckBlockHeader's own comment says the timewarp rule is 'Testnet4 and regtest only'.
findings.we_do: `(and (eq bl:*network* :testnet4) ...)` -- regtest can never enforce the BIP94 rule, and there is no option to enable it.
findings.impact: No consensus effect on any live network (testnet4 is covered, mainnet/testnet3/signet correctly exempt). It blocks Core's functional tests for the timewarp mitigation from running against us on regtest, so that rule has no regtest-driven coverage.

findings.title: bumpfee's MarkReplaced writes `replaced_by_txid` only in memory — the marker is lost on restart
findings.core_does: CWallet::MarkReplaced sets wtx.mapValue["replaced_by_txid"], calls RefreshMempoolStatus, and then PERSISTS the tx record with `WalletBatch batch(GetDatabase()); batch.WriteTx(wtx)` — logging and returning false if the write fails. The marker survives a restart.
findings.we_do:
%bumpfee-helper mutates the in-memory alist only:
  (setf (wallet-tx-map-value old-wtx) (append (remove "replaced_by_txid" ...) (list (cons "replaced_by_txid" ...))))
There is no `wallet-write-tx` call. The NEW tx's "replaces_txid" IS persisted (via %wallet-commit-transaction -> wallet-add-to-wallet -> wallet-write-tx, wallet-tx.lisp:808-810), and wallet-tx-record-value (wallet-tx.lisp:256-277) does serialize arbitrary map-value pairs — so the write would have worked; it is simply never issued.
findings.impact: After any node restart the original (RBF-replaced, mempool-evicted) transaction loses its `replaced_by_txid` marker. Three consequences: (1) wallet-available-coins (wallet-coins.lisp:274-280) drops the `safeTx = false` hold that Core's spend.cpp:390-399 applies to replaced transactions, so the wallet will happily fund a new spend from an output of a transaction that has been replaced and can never confirm — exactly the reorg double-pay hazard Core's comment describes; (2) %bump-precondition-checks (psbt.lisp:1698-1702) no longer refuses a second bump of the same transaction; (3) gettransaction/listtransactions silently stop reporting the field. Reproduce: bumpfee a tx, restart the node, then getbalance/listunspent shows the replaced tx's change as spendable and bumpfee accepts the same txid again.

findings.title: bumpfee forces fOverrideFeeRate, skipping the mempool-min-fee and required-fee halves of Core's CheckFeeRate
findings.core_does: CreateRateBumpTransaction copies the coin control and NEVER sets fOverrideFeeRate (the only two fOverrideFeeRate=true sites are rpc/spend.cpp:225 with override_min_fee and rpc/spend.cpp:570, neither reached by bumpfee). When the user supplies fee_rate it runs CheckFeeRate, which rejects newFeerate < chain().mempoolMinFee() (feebumper.cpp:67-75), new_total_fee < old_fee + incrementalRelayFee (:88-98), new_total_fee < GetRequiredFee (:100-105), and new_total_fee > maxtxfee (:107-113). GetMinimumFeeRate then still applies the GetRequiredFeeRate floor, and CreateTransactionInternal (spend.cpp:1160-1163) errors with "Fee rate (%s) is lower than the minimum fee rate setting (%s)".
findings.we_do: %create-rate-bump sets (wcc-override-feerate cc) t in BOTH branches. %wallet-minimum-fee-rate then returns early on the override (wallet-spend.lisp:339-342), skipping both the mempool-min-fee floor and the GetRequiredFeeRate floor, which also makes %create-transaction-internal's "Fee rate is lower than the minimum fee rate setting" guard unreachable. Only one of CheckFeeRate's four clauses is ported — the old_fee + incremental minTotalFee test at psbt.lisp:1796-1810 — plus the -maxtxfee cap inside %create-transaction-internal.
findings.impact: `bumpfee txid {"fee_rate": N}` with N below the node's dynamic mempool minimum (or below a raised -mintxfee) is accepted. The replacement is signed, committed to the wallet by %wallet-commit-transaction, and the original is marked replaced — but the mempool rejects it (broadcast failure is only logged, psbt.lisp:1867 / wallet-spend.lisp:2465-2468). The user is left with an unbroadcastable replacement holding the original's coins (IsSpent is true for them, wallet-coins.lisp:46-56) and an original marked replaced, i.e. the funds are stuck until abandontransaction. Core refuses before any of that happens. Reachable whenever the mempool min fee has risen above 1 sat/vB, since the ported minTotalFee clause only ever enforces roughly the incremental relay rate.

findings.title: ECDSA satisfaction sized at 72 bytes on a stated justification that is factually false — our signer does grind low-R
findings.core_does: MaxSatisfactionWeight is called with use_max_sig = !can_grind_r || UseMaxSig(txin, coin_control), and CanGrindR() is `!IsWalletFlagSet(WALLET_FLAG_DISABLE_PRIVATE_KEYS)`. So for any ordinary descriptor wallet holding private keys, every ECDSA satisfaction is sized at 71 bytes (descriptor.cpp:1163 `use_max_sig ? 72 : 71`); 72 is used only for watch-only wallets and for externally-selected inputs.
findings.we_do: +ecdsa-max-sig-size+ is a hard 72 everywhere, justified by the header comment "our signer produces RFC6979 signatures WITHOUT low-R grinding, so ~half of all signatures are 72 bytes". That premise is wrong: src/crypto/secp256k1.lisp:309-352 implements Core's exact CKey::Sign grind loop (incrementing 4-byte LE extra entropy until compact[0] < 0x80) and its own docstring says it is byte-identical to CKey::Sign(grind=true). Core's flag is also not about whether we grind but about WALLET_FLAG_DISABLE_PRIVATE_KEYS, which we never consult here.
findings.impact: Every estimated input is 1 byte (legacy: 4 weight units = 1 vB; segwit: 1 WU = 0.25 vB) larger than Core's. Because %create-transaction-internal fixes current_fee to fee_needed = effective_feerate x estimated_vsize and tops the change up to match, that overestimate is paid to the miner, not returned: a 500-input legacy consolidation at 100 sat/vB overpays ~50,000 sat. It also perturbs effective values and therefore coin selection versus Core. Always in the safe direction, but the stated reason for the divergence no longer holds and the constant should be 71 for private-key wallets.

findings.title: PSBT signing never checks that existing signatures use the requested sighash type
findings.core_does: After resolving the effective sighash, SignPSBTInput validates every signature ALREADY in the input against it: with SIGHASH_DEFAULT, m_tap_key_sig and every m_tap_script_sigs entry must be exactly 64 bytes; otherwise each must be 65 bytes ending in the sighash byte, and every partial_sigs entry must end in the sighash byte. Any mismatch returns PSBTError::SIGHASH_MISMATCH and no signature is added.
findings.we_do: %psbt-effective-sighash ports only the PSBT_IN_SIGHASH-vs-parameter comparison (psbt.lisp:1080-1083). The block that inspects the existing +psbt-in-partial-sig+ / +psbt-in-tap-key-sig+ / +psbt-in-tap-script-sig+ records has no counterpart: %psbt-record-signatures goes straight from the sighash resolution to %compute-input-signatures and records our signature alongside whatever was already there.
findings.impact: walletprocesspsbt will co-sign an input where a counterparty's partial signature uses a different sighash type (e.g. SIGHASH_NONE or ANYONECANPAY) without warning, where Core aborts the whole call with "Specified sighash and sighash in PSBT do not match". Core documents this block as "For user safety"; losing it removes the only signal an operator gets that the other participants in a multisig are not committing to the same transaction fields they are.

findings.title: PSBT "complete" and the already-signed test trust final/partial fields without verifying the scripts
findings.core_does: CWallet::FillPSBT computes `complete` as the AND of PSBTInputSignedAndVerified(psbtx, i, &txdata) over every input, which resolves the spent output and runs VerifyScript over final_script_sig/final_script_witness with a real MutableTransactionSignatureChecker under STANDARD_SCRIPT_VERIFY_FLAGS. SignPSBTInput uses the same predicate at :407 to decide an input needs no further work.
findings.we_do: %psbt-input-signed-p returns true on the mere PRESENCE of +psbt-in-final-scriptsig+ or +psbt-in-final-scriptwitness+, and %psbt-signer-result derives `complete` from %psbt-finalize-in-place on a copy — i.e. from whether the finalizer can assemble something, never from whether the assembled input verifies. (The create/commit paths do run %verify-tx-scripts, wallet-spend.lisp:1831-1860, but the PSBT RPC path does not.)
findings.impact: walletprocesspsbt / descriptorprocesspsbt can report complete:true and hand back a `hex` transaction that fails script verification — e.g. a PSBT arriving with a garbage final_scriptSig on one of our inputs (which we then skip signing entirely), or a multisig whose co-signer supplied a malformed partial signature that our finalizer still assembles. The user broadcasts and the node rejects it; Core would have reported complete:false and re-signed.

findings.title: No -walletcrosschain guard: a wallet whose locator belongs to another chain is loaded and rewritten
findings.core_does: AttachChain, unless -walletcrosschain is set, reads the stored best-block locator and refuses to load when locator.vHave.back() (the wallet's known genesis) differs from chain.getBlockHash(0): "Wallet files should not be reused across chains. Restart bitcoind with -walletcrosschain to override."
findings.we_do: wallet-attach-chain reads the stored locator only to call find-fork-in-active-chain; a locator from a foreign chain simply yields no fork, rescan-height falls to 0, and the wallet is attached, rescanned from its birthday, and its best-block record overwritten with the new chain's locator.
findings.impact: With a shared -walletdir (*wallet-directory* accepts an absolute path, wallet.lisp:324-338), opening a mainnet wallet on testnet/signet is accepted instead of refused. Every stored confirmed transaction is demoted to :inactive by %wtx-update-state-from-chain (wallet-tx.lisp:1222-1233), the balance reads as zero-and-pending, wallet-post-load-resubmit tries to push the foreign chain's transactions into this node's mempool, and the persisted best-block locator is replaced with the wrong chain's. Recoverable by reopening on the right chain (which rescans from the birthday), but Core's whole point is that the operator is told rather than shown a wallet that looks emptied.

findings.title: BIP143/BIP341 sighash writes nVersion through buf-set-u32-le, which is declared (unsigned-byte 32) while transaction-version is (signed-byte 32)
findings.core_does: SignatureHash (WITNESS_V0) does `ss << txTo.version` and SignatureHashSchnorr does `ss << tx_to.version` (interpreter.cpp:1520); CTransaction::version is int32_t and is serialized as plain two's-complement LE. Nothing in consensus restricts nVersion -- refs/bitcoin/src/consensus/tx_check.cpp CheckTransaction has no version rule at all; the only version range check is POLICY, in IsStandardTx (refs/bitcoin/src/policy/policy.cpp:101, `tx.version > TX_MAX_STANDARD_VERSION || tx.version < TX_MIN_STANDARD_VERSION`). So a miner may mine a transaction whose nVersion has bit 31 set (int32 negative) and every node must validate its segwit/taproot inputs.
findings.we_do: compute-bip143-sighash-real (interop.lisp:1858-1860) and compute-bip341-sighash-real (interop.lisp:3195-3197) both pass `(bl.ser:transaction-version tx)` -- a slot declared `(version 1 :type (signed-byte 32))` in src/serialization/types.lisp:152, filled by `br-read-i32-le` at types.lisp:214 -- into `buf-set-u32-le`, whose generating macro declares `(type (unsigned-byte 32) v)` under `(optimize (speed 3) (safety 1))` (src/util/bytes.lisp:41-51, instantiated at :54). The legacy sighash does NOT have this problem: compute-legacy-sighash uses `bb-write-u32-le` (interop.lisp:1660), whose macro masks with `(logand v #xffffffff)` and whose docstring at src/util/bytes.lisp:126-133 says in so many words that `a strict (unsigned-byte 32) declaration would break sighash on any tx with a negative version`. The same hazard was fixed for the byte-buf writers and left in place on the positional writers the BIP143/BIP341 preimages use.
findings.impact: Any miner can include, for the cost of one transaction, a block containing a P2WPKH/P2WSH/P2TR spend inside a transaction with nVersion >= 0x80000000. Core validates it normally. We hand a negative integer to a routine that declares its argument unsigned at safety 1: either SBCL signals a TYPE-ERROR out of the middle of validate-input-script (which has no handler in validate-tx-scripts / validate-block-scripts) -- an abort on a block Core accepts, i.e. a chain split plus a remote-triggerable validation error from any miner -- or, where the check is elided, the shift/mask arithmetic happens to be correct and nothing breaks. I could not execute the image (see coverage note) to determine which, but the divergence between the declaration and the actual slot type is unambiguous in the source, and the project's own sibling macro documents the failure it causes.

findings.title: *last-checksig-error* / *last-checkmultisig-error* are process-global specials, never rebound, so parallel script-check workers clobber each other's encoding verdict
findings.core_does: The encoding verdict is per-invocation state: EvalChecksigPreTapscript writes it into the caller's `ScriptError* serror` and returns false immediately (`if (!CheckSignatureEncoding(vchSig, flags, serror) || !CheckPubKeyEncoding(...)) return false;`). Each EvalScript call owns its own serror; Core's CCheckQueue workers share nothing of the kind.
findings.we_do: verify-checksig-for-script does `(setf *last-checksig-error* nil)` then `(setf *last-checksig-error* error-type)` on a plain defvar (interop.lisp:2207-2219), and the Coalton OP_CHECKSIG handler reads it back through last-checksig-had-strictenc-error-p (interop.lisp:2221-2223; read at src/coalton/script.lisp:1908-1913) to decide between pushing false and hard-failing the script. Neither this variable nor *last-checkmultisig-error* (interop.lisp:2323) is `let`-bound anywhere in src/ or tests/ -- I grepped both trees -- so under SBCL every setf writes the global value shared by all threads. src/validation/block.lisp:988-1016 runs validate-tx-scripts on a persistent worker pool.
findings.impact: With -parallelvalidation on (bl:*parallel-block-validation*), worker A's STRICTENC/DERSIG/NULLFAIL verdict is visible to worker B between B's own set and read. Two directions, both consensus-visible: B's valid CHECKSIG becomes a hard SE-VerifyFailed because A left an error set (a valid block rejected), or A's `nil` reset erases B's real encoding error so B pushes false instead of failing the script (a script Core rejects with SIG_DER/PUBKEYTYPE evaluates on, and `<sig> CHECKSIG NOT` style branches then succeed). This is the same class the project already fixed one layer up for *flag-set-cache* (interop.lisp:943-962) and for the coins view in #462; these two globals were missed.

findings.title: FindAndDelete is skipped for an EMPTY signature; Core's pattern for an empty sig is the single byte 0x00 (OP_0), not the empty script
findings.core_does: Both OP_CHECKSIG (EvalChecksigPreTapscript, interpreter.cpp:328-333) and OP_CHECKMULTISIG (interpreter.cpp:1141-1150) build the delete pattern as `CScript() << vchSig`. For an empty vchSig, CScript::AppendDataSize (refs/bitcoin/src/script/script.h:407-410) takes the `size < OP_PUSHDATA1` branch and inserts a single 0x00 byte, so the pattern is [0x00] -- one byte, not empty. FindAndDelete's early-out is `if (b.empty()) return 0` (interpreter.cpp:231), which does not fire, so every OP_0 sitting at an opcode boundary in scriptCode is deleted, and with SCRIPT_VERIFY_CONST_SCRIPTCODE `found > 0` is SCRIPT_ERR_SIG_FINDANDDELETE.
findings.we_do: strip-sigs-from-script-code maps an empty signature to `((zerop siglen) nil)` (interop.lisp:2405) and skips it entirely, and verify-checksig returns at interop.lisp:2055 before reaching its own find-and-delete whenever the signature is empty. We therefore never delete OP_0 from scriptCode and never raise :sig-findanddelete for an empty sig.
findings.impact: Relay-only. A legacy or P2SH script that carries OP_0 as an opcode in the scriptCode and passes an empty signature to CHECK(MULTI)SIG is non-standard to Core (SIG_FINDANDDELETE under CONST_SCRIPTCODE, a STANDARD flag) and standard to us, so we accept and relay a transaction every Core node refuses. Not a consensus split: an empty signature forces the CHECK(MULTI)SIG result to false in both implementations regardless of the mutated scriptCode, and CONST_SCRIPTCODE is not in either MANDATORY_SCRIPT_VERIFY_FLAGS or our block flag set.

findings.title: CONST_SCRIPTCODE's OP_CODESEPARATOR rule is applied only to the scriptPubKey and to a scriptCode reached by a CHECKSIG, not to the scriptSig or the P2SH redeem script
findings.core_does: The check lives inside EvalScript's opcode loop and is ungated by fExec: `if (opcode == OP_CODESEPARATOR && sigversion == SigVersion::BASE && (flags & SCRIPT_VERIFY_CONST_SCRIPTCODE)) return set_error(serror, SCRIPT_ERR_OP_CODESEPARATOR);` (interpreter.cpp:474-476). EvalScript is called three times per legacy input -- scriptSig, scriptPubKey, and the P2SH redeem script (interpreter.cpp:2020, :2023, :2069) -- so any OP_CODESEPARATOR anywhere in any of the three, executed or not, is rejected.
findings.we_do: verify-script pre-scans only the scriptPubKey for 0xab (interop.lisp:804-818, `Step 0a: CONST_SCRIPTCODE pre-check on scriptPubKey`). The only other place we look is verify-checksig's scan of `(or *current-script-code* script-pubkey)` at interop.lisp:2091-2112, which runs only when a CHECKSIG actually executes and only sees the scriptCode from the last codeseparator onward -- so a codeseparator in the scriptSig, in a P2SH redeem script, or in a branch with no CHECKSIG after it is never seen.
findings.impact: Relay-only divergence: a legacy/P2SH spend whose scriptSig or redeemScript contains OP_CODESEPARATOR without a following executed CHECKSIG is non-standard to Core and standard to us, so we relay a transaction the network drops. CONST_SCRIPTCODE is policy (it is in our +standard-policy-flags+ at src/validation/block.lisp:263 and never in the block flag set), so no consensus consequence.

findings.title: verify-checksig's inline FindAndDelete pattern omits the PUSHDATA prefix for signatures longer than 75 bytes
findings.core_does: `FindAndDelete(scriptCode, CScript() << vchSig)` -- CScript::AppendDataSize (script.h:407-424) emits `<len>` for sizes below 76, `OP_PUSHDATA1 <len>` for 76..255 and `OP_PUSHDATA2 <lo> <hi>` above that, so the pattern for a 76-byte signature is `4c 4c <76 bytes>`.
findings.we_do: `(let ((siglen (length sig-bytes))) (if (<= siglen 75) (concatenate ... (vector siglen) sig-bytes) sig-bytes))` (interop.lisp:2147-2152, and the same shape in the CONST_SCRIPTCODE probe at :2116) -- for a signature over 75 bytes we search for the bare signature bytes with no push opcode at all, which is neither Core's pattern nor a valid push encoding. Note strip-sigs-from-script-code (interop.lisp:2403-2415), used by the CHECKMULTISIG path, gets all three encodings right; only this single-CHECKSIG path is wrong.
findings.impact: No consensus consequence today: a >75-byte signature always fails IsValidSignatureEncoding, and DERSIG has been mandatory on every block since BIP66 activation, so the scriptCode mutated by this pattern is only ever used for a verification that is already doomed. It is a latent correctness defect in a consensus-critical helper and it makes the two FindAndDelete call sites in the same file disagree with each other.

findings.title: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY / OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY consult DISCOURAGE_UPGRADABLE_NOPS when their own flag is off; Core treats them as a plain NOP
findings.core_does: `case OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY: { if (!(flags & SCRIPT_VERIFY_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY)) { /* not enabled; treat as a NOP2 */ break; } ... }` (interpreter.cpp:521-526) and the identical shape for OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY at :560-565. Neither consults SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_UPGRADABLE_NOPS -- that flag is checked only in the OP_NOP1/OP_NOP4..OP_NOP10 case at interpreter.cpp:594-599. The `if (flags & DISCOURAGE_UPGRADABLE_NOPS)` inside the CLTV branch was removed from Core years ago.
findings.we_do: `((OP-CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY) (if (not (flag-enabled "CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY")) (check-discouraged-nop ctx) ...))` at src/coalton/script.lisp:2107-2110, and the same at :2141-2144 for CSV. check-discouraged-nop (script.lisp:1065-1073) returns SE-DiscourageUpgradableNops whenever DISCOURAGE_UPGRADABLE_NOPS is set.
findings.impact: No practical consequence under our current flag sets: block flags never carry DISCOURAGE_UPGRADABLE_NOPS (src/validation/block.lisp:255-268 puts it in +standard-policy-flags+ only) and the standard set always carries CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY and CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, so the two conditions never co-occur. It is a divergence a future flag-set change would expose silently, and script_tests.json has no vector covering the combination (I checked -- line 248 exercises the NOPs without the DISCOURAGE flag), so the green suite is not evidence.

findings.title: script-is-push-only-p rejects OP_RESERVED (0x50); Core's IsPushOnly deliberately counts it as push-type
findings.core_does: `bool CScript::IsPushOnly(const_iterator pc) const { while (pc < end()) { opcodetype opcode; if (!GetOp(pc, opcode)) return false; // Note that IsPushOnly() *does* consider OP_RESERVED to be a push-type opcode, however execution of OP_RESERVED fails, so it's not relevant to P2SH/BIP62 as the scriptSig would fail prior to the P2SH special validation code being executed. if (opcode > OP_16) return false; } return true; }` (script.cpp:266-281). OP_RESERVED is 0x50 <= OP_16 (0x60), so Core returns true for it; the source comment is explicit that this is intentional.
findings.we_do: `;; OP_RESERVED (0x50) - NOT a push / ((= op #x50) (return-from script-is-push-only-p nil))` at interop.lisp:1352-1355, called by verify-script for both the SIGPUSHONLY check (interop.lisp:823) and the BIP16 P2SH push-only requirement (interop.lisp:830-832).
findings.impact: Error-code only, no accept/reject divergence: Core reaches its IsPushOnly call for P2SH only after EvalScript(scriptSig) succeeded, and an executed OP_RESERVED is SCRIPT_ERR_BAD_OPCODE there (it falls to interpreter.cpp:1217-1218's default), so the script fails either way -- which is exactly what the Core comment says. We report :sig-pushonly where Core reports BAD_OPCODE. Worth fixing because the predicate is also the shape a future caller would reuse.

findings.title: OP_CHECKMULTISIG charges nKeysCount against the 201-op budget only after running the signature verifications; Core charges and enforces it before
findings.core_does: Immediately after reading nKeysCount and range-checking it: `nOpCount += nKeysCount; if (nOpCount > MAX_OPS_PER_SCRIPT) return set_error(serror, SCRIPT_ERR_OP_COUNT);` (interpreter.cpp:1116-1121) -- before the FindAndDelete loop and before the verification `while` loop, so a script that busts the budget costs zero ECDSA verifications.
findings.we_do: execute-opcode runs do-checkmultisig-stack-op -- which performs the whole multisig including every ECDSA verification -- and only then computes `(+ (context-op-count ctx) n-pubkeys)` and compares it against +max-ops-per-script+ (src/coalton/script.lisp:1980-1994 for CHECKMULTISIG, :2028-2040 for CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY). The op-count is also not charged at all on the :error / :underflow / :pubkey-count / :sig-count paths.
findings.impact: Resource-only, and small: the accept/reject verdict is identical because every path that skips the charge already returns an error, and the over-budget case still returns SE-TooManyOps. The cost is that we run up to MAX_PUBKEYS_PER_MULTISIG (20) signature verifications that Core never performs, on a script Core rejects for free. Cheap DoS amplification on a validation path an attacker controls via a P2SH redeem script.
